maintopic: AIDS TO NAVIGATION ON VANCOUVER -SKAGWAY ROUTE.

speechtext: On the Orders of the Day:

maintopic: AIDS TO NAVIGATION ON VANCOUVER -SKAGWAY ROUTE.
speechtext: May I ask the Minister of Marine whether negotiations are preceding with the United States Government regarding further aids to navigation on the route between Vancouver and Skagway, Alaska? I have in mind the wreck of the Princess Sophia off the Lynn canal last October.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
maintopic: AIDS TO NAVIGATION ON VANCOUVER -SKAGWAY ROUTE.
speechtext: No negotiations are going on at the present time between the Canadian Government and the Government of the United States with regard to that part of the coast on which the United .States have to provide the necessary aids to navigation. The unfortunate accident to the Princess Sophia on the Vanderbilt Ledge occurred on a part of the coast which is under the control of the United States Government; Canada has no jurisdiction over it. The Canadian coast, line extends northward to the entrance to Portland canal, near Port Simpson; follows the Portland canal to the head, and thence proceeds in a northwesterly direction inland. South of the International boundary the inland waterway is well marked; indeed there are very few representations in that regard from shipping interests that remain unsatisfied. Every reasonable endeavour is made to meet requirements as they arise. Northward of Port Simpson the inland waterway lies in United States territory, the point where the Princess Sophia was lost being about 350 miles up the coast north of the International boundary.

On section 8-Porcupine Forest Reserve No. 1:

maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Just what area is being taken out of this Reserve?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: The Porcupine Reserve in the province of Manitoba covers an area of 777-5 square miles, and we are taking out of that 2-5 square miles. Out of the Porcupine Reserve in Saskatchewan we are taking 376-5 square miles which will reduce the present area of the reserve in Saskatchewan from 3,246-75 to 2,870-25.

maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: How far from a railway will settlement be permitted in these reserves?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: We have not adopted any rigid rule in that regard. While the reserve remains as such, there is necessarily no railway penetration, there being no need for railway service; but when these areas are taken out and settled, there will be need of railway service. Portions of the area we are taking out will doubtless be a considerable distance from a railway. The river-I forget its name-has to be traversed, and doubtless bridges will have to be built. The soldiers are very anxious to settle on this area and take their chances of a railway going in. I think the hon. member for Dauphin or the hon. member for Nelson could give the distance from the railway better than I could.

maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: As I understand it, in the area that is being taken out, the shortest distance to the railway will 6 or 7 miles, running from 15 to 20 miles, and perhaps more, in other portions.

maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
Are the lots being taken out in a solid block or being, selected because of their suitability for agricultural purposes? My reason for asking is that where areas are selected through
a forest reserve, and settlement is created within the reserve, there is very great danger of the reserve being entirely wiped out by fire.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Areas are not being taken out in any regular blocks. The first principle followed is this: The land must be reasonably fit for agricultural purposes or mixed farming. It must be found to be so, and we have tried to be very careful in that regard, because this reserve was first created on the assumption that it was more fit for forestry than anything else. We have had to exercise considerable caution not to be over-influenced by those anxious to settle on forest reserves, because very frequently they hastily come to the conclusion that it is agricultural land when really it is not. However, after the most careful survey we could make of this Porcupine reserve, which is the principal one we are dealing with in this Bill, we came to the conclusion that we could not justify retaining this area. What we are taking out is in two pieces. I cannot describe it better than by showing it to the hon. member on the map. The portion to the west is oblong in shape and about two townships wide, varying somewhat on the northern limit. I he other portion is almost square in shape, situated more to the east, and is about twenty miles from the eastern boundary of the province of Saskatchewan.

maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: I chance to be familiar with that part of the country. The area which is being taken out in Saskatchewan is south of the lower Red Deer river and southeast of Etomami Junction. It at one time formed the famous reserve owned by one of our worthy senators. It was covered with magnificent spruce, but in 1886 the reserve was burnt, and a second fire cleaned the timber right off. There is now no timber on it, and nearly every foot of it is fit for farming.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: I can more fully answer my hon. friend from Pontiac now. The large portion taken out of the Porcupine reserve runs in an oblong shape east and west. The Canadian Northern railway runs east and west along the north part of it, distant about seven or eight miles from the northern extremity of the excepted area. The excepted area is, generally speaking, about twelve miles deep. Very little of the land that is being taken out of the reserve is more than nineteen miles distant from a railway, and the average would be about twelve or thirteen miles.

maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: About four square miles are taken out of this reserve for soldiers' settlement.

maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Is this land to be thrown open to soldiers for home settlement?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: DOMINION FOREST RESERVES AND PARKS ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
The method we have
under consideration, and which I think will be carried out, will be to permit only soldier entry in the reserve. That is to say no one except a soldier can go in, and the soldier cannot get a homestead; all he can get

is soldier entry, or the soldier homestead. The right to his other homestead will still remain intact. What we contemplate is to enable the soldier to take soldier entry of 160 acres in that reserve, and reserve 80 acres that adjoins in each case, so that if he makes good in the quarter-section we will subsequently let him have the 80 acres, probably by sale. It will possibly not be at full value but on terms that will be afterwards made known. In the meantime it is intended to make some provision by which he will have the use of that 80 acres. That is what the Soldiers' Settlement Board now have in mind. The scheme may be modified if it is deemed wise but at present we contemplate giving him a soldier entry there and reserving 80 acres for his use. Subsequently the land can be owned by him if he shows success as a farmer.

speechtext:
That is a difficult problem. In homesteading, so far the first man has always got entiy. There are the gravest possible objections to that system, particularly in its application to soldiers, because in its ultimate operation in regard to soldiers it means that a man physically incapacitated by service is at a serious disadvantage. That is its fatal objection as applicable to soldiers and the board is considering, and will have power in the matter if the Soldiers' Settlement Act which is now before the House is passed, the adopting of another method, that of granting entry by lot. I do not particularly like that method, but I really am not able to think of anything better. There is no way by which any priority can be given on the part of the board which would be considered fair or acceptable, and the board is of the opinion

that the matter will have to be worked out on the lot principle in some way.

speechtext: While I recognize the difficulty that tlhe minister points out, I may say- that this matter was brought to the attention of the Government largely through the efforts of certain returned soldiers who were particularly familiar with that district. The returned soldiers who went from the Dauphin district, and who had been up there and gone through the district on several occasions, brought this matter to the attention of the board. The father of one of these soldiers had been a squatter for some years. The point I wish to bring to the attention of the minister is this: Considering the work done by these soldiers, and the efforts made by them resulting in the whole of the land being thrown open, it is a question whether some consideration should not be given to them. They have done work which should be recognized in some way, and if they are just given the same terms and conditions as others it would hardly seem fair or right. I recognize the difficulty there is, but I desire to make a plea for these particular people.

House again in Committee on Bill No. 19, to consolidate and amend the Railway Act-Mr. Boivin in the Chair. (Resumed from May 28).
On section 374-consent of municipality for transmission lines upon highways, etc.:

I have an amendment to move to subsection 5 of section 374 by striking out that subsection and making a substitution which I will explain as I proceed. The Senate has seen flit to alter the Bill as it left this House in 1917 so as to favour a particular group of electrical companies. They favour one company but really they favour a group of interlocking companies. The result of the amendment which appears in the Bill now before the Committee is that the special legislative bargain made in 1902, when the private Act of the Toronto Niagara Power Company was passed by this House, is
annulled and has no effect. For these reasons I wish to take the opinion of the Committee as to restoring the course agreed upon by the House in 1917.
The matter has now been before members for some weeks; in fact, I might say for some years and in a case of this kind where definitely the rights of the public, as represented by the municipalities, come into collision with the private, corporate rights of those in a certain business, it must, and always does, follow that the case of the municipalities, being so widely distributed and the interests so general, does not receive the attention which is given to the other side of the case by large corporations who keep a close rwatch on legislation as a matter of business. The public has little or no machinery by which to use its persuasive powers on members of Parliament or otherwise, but fortunately there have always been in this House a number ot members quick to discern what is in the interest of the public as against -a special or private interest and to see that the public interest is protected. Members of Parliament have always been careful to study enactments proposed in order to see that public rights shall not be surrendered. Ordinary vigilance really is the price oi liberty where great monetary interests are concerned and here we have, as I shall show in a minute or two, a charter which is to be given by this special clause contained in the amendment of the Senate which will be worth many millions of dollars-one cannot help saying that-and which will allow one company, or group of companies, to extend their operations not only in Ontario where they at present are but throughout the whole Dominion. It will be a charter which will allow exploitation in every province of the Dominion. While the companies concerned are now only operating in one province, yet the advantage gained by -this amendment would be so obvious that they would have little difficulty in getting capital to proceed with operations in other provinces.
It might be thought that it is not necessary to go into the details of this matter because it has been so much discussed, but I find that in this-discussion it is wonderful how some members only get the point of view of one person with whom they discussed the case, while another member only gets some other point of view. These views are disjointed, and in the committee of which I was a member and which reported this Bill as it is, there were a number of members who said that they thought they



understood the question before the committee and that they never imagined that so many arguments could be advanced on the side which they had made up their minds did not have the best of it. However, I have come to a conclusion upon the rights and wrongs of the parties opposed to each other in connection with this Bill without regard to the advocacy of any interest, and I deem it my duty to give the committee the benefit of the reasons which assisted me in reaching that conclusion. Late last session, for the purpose of getting at the bottom of it, I looked into the matter very carefully, I have come to a certain conclusion as the result of that investigation and I think it only proper, for the benefit of those who have not studied the matter closely, to give the House a short history oi the matter and to point out the importance of the principle involved in this legislation.
The whole trouble arose really from a slip in the drafting of the statute. Our law clerk drew the statute in 1902 which formed the charter of the Toronto and Niagara Power company. So far so good, but our law clerk, when this statute came to be revised in 1903, forgot, or erred, in not looking after the rights of the public which were secured in the charter of the company. Lay members, of course, probably as well as lawyers, must know that from time to time the statutes of Canada, as of every other country, must, for public convenience, be revised and consolidated. Constant amendments are being made. It is very difficult, not only for the ordinary citizen, but for the practitioner, to go through all the statute-books and ascertain exactly what the law is.
So that at certain periods-it has been at intervals of twenty years in the Dominion, and at shorter intervals in the provinces-the public statutes have been revised and consolidated to make them more readable and more convenient for reference. So with the Railway Act which was known as the Railway Act of 1888 but which in 1903 was revised under the Railway Act of that year. The reason I say that our law clerk made a slip in legislation which, if we allow it to pass and to go uncorrected, will mean taking a great public right away from those to whom it was promised, is, that he neglected to carry into the Railway Act of 1903 the provisions of the special charter of the company taken from the Railway Act of 1899. So we come to this state of affairs: That Parliament passed in 1902 this charter which was satisfactory to both parties; then in 1903, the Railway Act being about to be consolidated, the draftsman,
[Mr. Mowat.l
as is usual in these cases, inserted a clause that all previous Railway Acts should be repealed. Well, that was all very well, that was good enough if there had been brought forward into the new Consolidated Railway Act all the rights given to persons by the Act which had been repealed. I have no doubt that the law clerk thought he did so, but it might have been well if, at the time he was drawing the Consolidated Act in 1903, which repealed all previous Acts, the parties concerned, at any rate the public, had been represented, and that when he drew the clause to repeal the Act of 1899, under which the public rights were granted, the public guardian had said: Stay your hand; remember that under the Act of 1899 the public were given great privileges; be careful that you do not so consolidate the new Act and repeal the old Act as to take those rights away. If that had been done this contest would never have occurred. But unfortunately it did not occur to the law clerk that by repealing the former Railway Act of 1899 any such effect was being brought about. Such is the situation, however, and it is now being declared that the Act of 1899 does not control the Toronto, and Niagara Power Company.
Before I continue this branch of the subject let me say that we are not asking in the amendment to do anything which is unprecedented, or to take away rights which have been granted; we are only asking that the will of Parliament, clearly expressed in 1902, seventeen years ago, should obtain and be declared so as to govern the parties to this controversy at the present time. It is said that other interests and rights have intervened since that time which changed the condition of affairs. Let me say that Parliament has never been guided by any such principle at all, but has seemed anxious in the passing of corporate legislation to do what was right as between the corporations and the public that they serve. An instance of that is to be found in the amendment to the Bell Telephone Act of 1906. The Bell Telephone Company, it will be remembered, enjoyed great rights at first. The telephone was a new thing, and the public were anxious to have it in their shops and homes, and they did not know exactly what would be the result of a telephone company suddenly descending upon a town and doing its own will on the streets of that community without regard to the convenience of the people, or the rights of the council, or of a city or town engineer, to control those streets. iSo sure were the

*Bell Telephone 'Company of their rights' in this respect that they started to do work in the city of Toronto, interfering with the general rights of the public over their streets. Litigation ensued, the
4 p.m. case went to the Privy Council, and that tribunal held that the Bell Telephone Company under its charter, had the right to do what it was doing without asking the consent of the municipal authorities. This made all the more acute the feeling on the part of the municipal authorities throughout Canada, and their champions in Parliament, and rendered it all the more imperative that everything must be done to" guard municipal rights in regard to these big utility corporations. The consequence was that when the Bell Telephone Company came to Parliament in 1906 for an amendment to its charter, and to ask that the capital should be increased -not a very great desideratum* one would think-Parliament immediately took the opportunity to make a condition that the very same provision that had been inserted in the Act of the Toronto and Niagara Power Company should be embodied in the Bell Telephone Act of 1906. Now it is undoubted that Parliament, by putting into the Bell Telephone Act the provision that the company must obtain the consent of the municipal authorities before they entered a town, to that extent interfered with the vested rights of that particular company. It cut down those rights in a very considerable degree, and at the same time declared the rights of other telephone companies who desired, or might desire hereafter, to deal with the municipalities. It must have had that effect, nevertheless the Bell Telephone Company apparently submitted. I notice by reading Hansard of 1906 that the Bell Telephone Company Bill was in charge of the hon. member for Three Rivers (iMr. Bureau) and it was evidently intended to wangle the Bill through without this particular clause; but in the end the cham- . pions of public rights in Parliament, one of .whom was Mr. Justice Lennox, then the representative for South Simcoe, and .another Mr. W. F. Maclean, member for .South York, sturdily opposed the passage ,of the Bill, until it was made perfectly clear that the Railway Act should apply to the Bell Telephone Company. The clause which was inserted at that time into the Bell Telephone Company Act is as follows:
Chapter 61, Acts of 1906:
This Act and the Bell Telephone Company of Canada shall be subject to the provisions of the Railway Act 3 903, and amendments thereto,
1954	'
Here we have this well studied and deliberately determined upon precedent, that the rights of the public are to be considered and that vested rights cannot prevail against them. That is the principle that I ask the Committee to-day to re-adopt.
Taking the particular case in which we are interested to-day, it is that of the To-ronto-Niagara Power Company which came to Parliament in 1902 and obtained corporate powers which were conceded by its advocates before the special committee on the Railway Bill, and which in fact, it is not disputed, are very generous and very ample. Those powers are very wide powers, largely no doubt owing to the fact that the people who obtained this Act were pioneers in the transmission of electric energy from Niagara Falls, and it was not then manifest what their attitude towards the public might be. The very fact that such full, generous, and ample powers were granted under this charter should make us, it seems to me, all the more careful that the rights of this company should be confined and restricted to the statute which was then passed, and which should not be departed from
If they got so much sweet out of the bargain, they must take what they consider is the sour part, for that is the only way in which justice can be done. I argue that the Act was the result of a distinct and special legislative bargain. Legislative bargains between Parliament and the promoters of a (Bill have always been noticed by the courts. /In fact, in this very Bell Telephone case that I have spoken of, reported in 1905 Appeal Cases, it will be seen that Lord Mac-nachten in discussing the Bill mentions the fact that the legislation was alleged to have been of the nature of a bargain; the Telephone Company asked for something, and conceded something, in order to get what is asked for; but he finds that there was not sufficient evidence of that to allow him to decide the point. Apparently he is quite of the opinion1-I only quote this as one of many cases-that if a legislative bargain was made plain to the court, the *court would not enforce any law which was abhorrent to that bargain.
I assert that this special Act was passed on the express understanding-more than that, on the express undertaking of the promoters-that the Railway Act of 1899- which gave very special privileges of control to municipalities-should be incorporated in it. Let me for a moment direct the attention of the Committee to section 21 of

the Company's Act, which provides that section 90 and sections 136 to 169, and so on, of the Railway Act are to apply to the company and its undertakings, "in so far as the said sections are not inconsistent with the provisions of this Act, and subject to the following: Wherever in the said Sections of the Railway Act the word 'company' occurs, it shall mean the power company hereby incorporated."
I emphasize that because of the reason that since this slip in the draftmanship which I mentioned, it has been held that the clauses which were referred to related only to railway companies, and not to a power company such as this, although it is quite clear here that Parliament said expressly that "power company" was what it meant when it provided that the clauses ol the 1899 Railway Act should apply and control and restrict this particular company.
What were the clauses of 'the Act of 1899 which were at the time incorporated in this clear language? They were very much as you find them in section 373 of this Bill which is before you as applicable to telephone companies, and rather than repeat them in section 374-the clause we are now considering-the draftsman in subsection 3 refers to section 373. And that was the reason for not setting out in the particular .Act of 1902 all the clauses of 'the Railway Act which were meant. to apply, it being more convenient to refer to 'the clauses.
When this company got its charter it got two things: a restriction in fevour of the municipalities as to control of their streets, and also another thing that vastly outweighed that in importance, namely, the power 'to expropriate property. That was a very important clause, and I wonder if, when it is contended here that the Railway Act of 1899, incorporated by this clause 21, is gone by reason of bad draftsmanship as regards the restrictive rights of the municipalities, it will be conceded that the expropriation rights of the company are also gone. I do not think so. You will find that a -company of this kind will fight to retain what is advantageous in its Aot, and it will fight to exclude everything that it thinks is disadvantageous.
One would imagine that the fairest way of dealing with the whole thing would be to cut out the expropriation clauses granted by this particular charter, -as it has been decided by the highest -court that bad draftsmanship has eliminated the restrictive clauses. If they are to be relieved of the restrictions they ought to give up the benefits. But, of course, we cannot, expect the

company to do so, and it would not bo business policy on their part.
Supposing clauses 136 to 169 inclusive had been -actually set out, that would have taken up several page-s of the statute book, and have made the charter very long. Therefore, it was generally felt at the time that it would be perfectly adequate for the purpose that the sections themselves should be simply referred to instead of being set out in extenso. I notice that in 1901-and I must give these things because 1 want ito be absolutely fair-the Ottawa and Hull Power Company was incorporated, and there the very same language was used, namely, that:
Section 90 of the Railway Act shall apply to the company, but no other provisions of the said Act shall apply thereto.
That is to say, they should have no expropriation rights such -as this Niagara Power Company got. In the same year the St. Lawrence Power -Company was incorporated, and the clause of the Railway Act was actually copied into the Special Act. If that had been done in this case we would not be here -at all discussing this matter. But simply because of the peculiar algebraic way in which the legislation was affected by reference to an Act which was afterwards repealed, it has been held that with the repeal of the Act-inadvertently, as I say-the whole restriction is gone.
I now come to the point as to whether there was a legislative bargain. In 1902 two members of the House of Commons, who were either specially deputed by the municipalities or were so of their own choice, were the champions of public rights. One of these was Edward F. Clarke, one of the members for Toronto, a man with whom I had the closest intimacy and business associations, because when he w.a.s mayor of Toronto-and a better mayor Toronto never had-I happened to be one of the city solicitors and it was my privilege to meet Mr Clarke many and many a time.
[DOT] 1 was impressed with the extraordinary Interest and zeal that- he showed in connection with one piece of legislation after another in favour of the rights of municipalities. He was the champion; he was the man who saw where some power cbuld come in and destroy the well-earned or well bought liberties of municipalities. Mr. Clarke was associated with Mr. E. B. Osier, now -Sir Edmund Osier, who was a little bit alarmed about section 90 when this Act went through; it was not his idea that section 90 should be mentioned as being included in

the Act. But Mr. Clarke said: Will it do any harm to set out in this charter exactly what the restrictive powers are in favour of the city engineer or the city or town council? But the very persons who insisted that this reference to the Railway Act was sufficient were the promoters of the Act; that is the important point to be kept in mind. It was not the clause of 'the municipalities; it was the clause of the promoters of this Act. Mr. Pringle, then the member for Stormont, who was in charge of the Bill and handled it with a great deal of ability, pointed out that the clause of the Railway Act was all-sufficient; that there was no necessity for spreading it out on the statute. Mr. Osier said, column 3629 of Hansard, 1902:
Would it do any harm to put in this simple clause stating that this charter shall he subject to all Acts that may be passed by this House referring to electrical companies of this kind?
The Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Sutherland) : There can be no doubt that it is.
Mr. Osier: ... If it is in the clause already, why not insert this and make it without any doubt?
Then Mr. M. K. Cowan, who was chairman of the special committee which considered this Bill, said:
When, this committee goes to erect poles or wires across the streets of Toronto it can only do so with the consent of the Municipal Council of that city, or of other municipalities in which it operates.
It is clear, therefore, that two members of 'the House, who were willing 'to take the word of lawyers in the committee-eminent counsel in charge of the Bill, and ministers of the Crown-thought that that was fair ground for letting 'the thing go through as it was. But in addition to that, Mr. Pringle after some discussion and some objections by Mr. Clarke, goes on to say, at column 3634:
Will the hon. gentleman allow me to put a question to him? The question I wish to put is: How this section 90 of the Railway Act, as amended in 1899, affects this question?
The amendment is as follows:
"When any company has power by any Act of Parliament to construct and maintain lines of telegraph or telephone or lines for the conveyance of light, heat, power or electricity, such company may with the consent of the municipal council or other authority having jurisdiction over any highway, square or other public place, enter thereon," etc.
I rather gather, from what the hon. gentleman says, that the section of the Act does not mean what it purports. Well, I understand that it means just what it expresses:	All
companies have to obtain consent of a municipality before passing through it. And I want
to ask, what is the effect on this question of section 90 of the Railway Act, as amended in 1899 ?
So that this section of the Act of 1899, which, we say, contained safeguards of the rights of the public, was put in there at the instance of the very company which is now seeking to destroy it by reason of a chance interpretation of the statute by the courts. But Parliament is above all courts. Parliament may express itself in a way to which the courts may seem inadequate, obscure, or in some other way objectionable, If so, all the courts have to do is direct attention to the matter. But to say that the Parlia-men of Canada should be subject to the opinions of the courts is, to my mind, absurd; we are the law-makers here, and all the courts have to do is to interpret the laws that we make. If, as a matter of law, the courts say that we have not said what we meant to say, or that we have left out something that should have been put in, we are willing to remedy the matter. But I utterly repudiate the suggestion that our action as law-makers is to be controlled by the courts. So that on the whole we have here a distinct legislative bargain. This Bill went through despite the objections of these two champions of the rights of the public, because they were assured that section 90 of the Railway Act applied. And everybody thought that it did apply-the promoters of the Act more than anybody else, because it was they who fathered the clause.
Inis company, under section 12 of its Act, have the right to distribute electricity, to become a merchant in that commodity to sell it to users of electricity, and they had also the right to shove their trunk lines through municipalities without distributing electricity to the people of those municipalities. They had these two rights and they never for a moment objected to the restrictive powers that were inserted in the statute of 1902.
Then comes along the revision of 1*03, repealing the Act of 1899. I may inform the laymen of the House, who may, perhaps, not he aware of it-I speak, of course, with reference to lawyers, because they knojv all about it-that the law is this: There is in every volume of revised or consolidated statutes a clause which says that the provisions of the repealed Act shall he carried on into the revised Act unless the contrary is expressed. Our last revision of the statutes was in 1906, and the way it is expressed in the interpretation clause of the revised statutes of Canada, 1906, section 1, is as follows:-

Whenever any Act is repealed or other provisions are substituted by way of consolidation, any reference in any unrepealed Act-
That is, this charter.
-to such repealed Act-
That is, the Railway Act of 1899.
*-as regards any subsequent transaction shalll be held and construed to a reference to the provisions of the substituted Act relating to the same subject matter as such repealed Act.
That is plain enough, is it not? One would have thought that when the Court of Appeal of Ontario-the Appellate Division, composed of five judges: Chief Justice Moss, Mr. Justice Garrow, Mr. Justice Magee, Mr. Justice Meredith, and Mr. Justice McLaren-held that it was plain enough that the revised statute did apply, the case would go no further; but it did. It went to the Privy Council, and it is because of the decision of the Privy Council, which wras the luckiest decision any litigant ever got in this world, that this aggregation of companies now comes here and puts their case in this way, as it seems to me: We got a statute in 1902 which said that we must get the consent of municipalities before we could put down our poles; we accepted that interpretation until 1911, and then we began litigation as the only thing to do; the little town of North Toronto, some four miles north of Toronto, objected to our running transmission lines along certain streets, and started to cut down our poles; we commenced litigation and we won twice; we got a decision in our favour, which now gives us vested rights.
I shall have to detain the Committee for a moment while we see what there is in that contention. When this aggregation of companies say that they have vested rights by the decision of the highest court in the realm, one would naturally suppose that that meant that both parties had come before the highest court of the realm and put the merits of their respective cases before that court. You would naturally suppose that that was the case; that by the decision of the highest court of the realm the case of one of the parties was declared to be predominant upon its merits and upon the law. But was that the case? Very far from it; in fact, it is just the contrary. What this aggregation of companies won in the Privy Council decision was nothing more than a judicial decision on statutes and words used by our law clerk; that is all. It was alleged that it was highly important that this company, which was a pioneer in the transmission of Niagara

power to the municipalities of Ontario, should not be impeded by having to ask the consent of municipalities through which they wanted to bring their lines, because some municipality, some miserable township it might be, might hold the company-up by refusing to give consent, and the enterprise would be ruined. That was put before the Privy Council. On the other hand, the case of the municipalities was put before the Privy Council, to the effect that it was more important in the interests of this Dominion that municipalities should have the right to make mistakes if they wanted to and refuse, if they desired, consent to this power company going through their territory. They might be very foolish and very backward in doing that, but they had the right to refuse consent, and the right to make that mistake, if mistake it was. What does the Privy Council say on these two contrary placings of the merits of the case before them. It says this (page 840):
Lord Haldane: If the powers conferred by this section (section 90) displaced the less restricted powers of entering- without any consent conferred toy the Act of Incorporation, the appellants (the power company) are in the wrong.
Your lordships have, therefore, to determine this question. They have to hear in mind that a court of justice is not entitled to speculate as to which" of two conflicting policies was intended to prevail, but must confine itself to the construction of the language of the relevant statutes read as a whole.
So that utterly precludes this aggregation of power companies from now saying that the decision of the Privy Council is in favour of their case on its merits. Because the Privy Council distinctly say: "We will not decide that; we will simply decide on the statutes." Any layman can see what an exceedingly narrow decision it was, and how it might just as well have been the other way. As it happened, the decision after running along the top of the fence, turned over to the corporate side. The decision was simply this. Their lordships said that while in this charter the Railway Act of 1899 is to apply, and where-ever the word "company" occurs in the Railway Act it shall mean the power company, yet that Act was repealed, so there was nothing for them to do but to look to the Act of 1903 which repealed it, and that Act of 1903, unfortunately, defined "company" not as a power company, but as a railway company. That is the whole basis of the decision of the Privy Council, and is the result of ineffective legislation of ours here in this House, and of our law clerk not being alert to save the rights given

Parliament. The precautions we took to say that "company" meant power company are wasted, because the Railway Act of 1903 the Consolidating Act, says that "company" means only railway company. Therefore, as this power company is not a railway company it is free of the restrictions we imposed in 1902.
So it seems to me obvious that we must go back and place ourselves in the position of our predecessors in 1902, who meant to do a certain thing, who were commissioned by the public to protect their rights, and who did protect their rights by certain legislation. We should have no hesitation whatever, no matter what vested rights have occurred, in going back and doing what was done in 1902, and doing what was done by this House in 1917. Personally, I very much doubt whether there are any very great vested interests which would be affected. How can any interests be affected by a change in. this section simply making effective the legislation of 1902? This corporation got its charter in 1902, and we never heard a word of this dispute until 1911. They agreed right up to that time that they had to get the consent of the municipality, and not only the consent, but a lot of other things set out in the statute of 1899. Older members of the House may . Temember how in the old days the Montreal Telegraph Company and the Dominion Telegraph Company, now consolidated, and the Bell Telephone Company, could put their poles through any town and do almost anything that they liked. There was absolutely no power to restrict them except that in one case they were obliged (to paint the poles. But that is a small thing. We all remember that particularly in one of the best streets in the city they erected poles with wires on them which were so low t-hat a man on top of a team load of hay could not pass under them. They would put up double lines of poles on one Street and would so construct the poles that the firemen could not get their ladders from the street to a burning building, and in many other ways they became a menace to the life of the public. From the time that the first power company was incorporated by this Parliament in 1895, twenty-four years ago, there constantly grew a feeling on the part of Parliament that the rights of municipalities were supreme. So that in all legislation following that, and in the Railway Act, it is provided that they must consult the municipalities, and traffic must not be obstructed. Wires must- be of a certain height
and poles must be perpendicular. In addition, there must be the right to cut down poles and wires in case of fire without any obligation to pay compensation, and trees must not be injured. My hon. friend from Gaspe told us in the Committee that one of the companies went into his place and cut down a beautiful tree and there was no recourse against them. I hope the hon. member will bear that in mind when he comes to vote on the amendment. It was also provided that the work on any street or square should be done under the city engineer, and that the workmen should wear badges and not go into private houses * without authority, and that temporary removal of wires and poles should be made if necessary. Twelve sub-clauses protecting'the rights of the municipalities are now absolutely swept away by this Senate amendment unless it is rejected by this House. I do not think that the cry of vested rights should swerve us from our duty in respect of this amendment. In 1902 the company got the power to go anywhere in Canada and issue bonds. They are now in Ontario, but the franchise is so valuable that if they win here we may expect them in the near future to be in every province where there is any waterpower at all. As I say, they got the power to go into any province and issue bonds to the extent of $1,500,000, and they did. In 1903, after they were incorporated by this charter, they sold out to another company, the Electrical Development Company, situate at Niagara Falls. That company took all their bonds of $1,500,000. So that so far as this company goes, its bonds are not affected because they are not in the stock markets. They -claim that that does not matter so long as they are linked up with some other company. However, the Electrical Company got their bonds -and was able to use the transmission company. They worked together, and afterwards there (was a company formed, another company which held no physical assets. They had no property, but held all the stock of the Electrical Company, the Toronto Niagara Power Company, and, I think, the Toronto Electric Light Company. This combination was called the Toronto Power Company. The Toronto Power Company in 1911 issued a mortgage on all the assets of all the companies of naminally $25,000,000, of which they issued $18,000,000. But before this question of the rights of municipalities and their intervention had come up at all, the aggregation of these power companies had issued bonds to the

extent of $7,800,000, or nearly half the whole amount of bonds issued. One would say that if they had issued, in round numbers, $8,000,000 of bonds on this charter, which everyone believed gave the municipalities their rights, they could not have got very much more after they got a decision of the Privy Council in 1912. They now say: We have certain rivals. There is a semi-public utility in Ontario called the Hydro-Electric Company, and they have become our rivals, and this question of consent means a great deal more than it did then, for the municipalities may link up with the Hydro and may not give consent. But that could not have occurred in 1911 when they issued these 'bonds. When a company wants to sell its bonds it employs a well-read, expert *counsel, a lawyer who is accustomed to commercial law. Without his opinion that under the statutes fhe basis of the bonds is good, they cannot possibly enter the stock market. But, suppose they asked Mr. Lash or any other good corporate lawyer for an opinion as to their bonds preparatory to going into the .stock market, what would Mr. Lasfh have found? He would have found, if it was previous to 1912, when they got this decision as to bad draftmanship, that the very charter under which they were acting incorporated the Railway het, which said that they had to get the consent of the municipalities. So that the public, who only look to the opinion of eminent counsel, would have only that information, and would have the right to say: "We gave you that charter only on condition that the municipalities had rights." But the answer is made: What does the public know about what occurred in Hansard and what Mr. 'Clark bargained for, or what Mr. Osier and Mr. Pringle said? They do not read Hansard and do not know anything about it. Well, the public may not read Hansard, but Mr. Lash knew all about the matter, 'because he and his friends had it put forward in Parliament, providing that the municipalities should have power to consent. Mr. Lash must therefore have known about it. Anyway, there it stares counsel in the face. He will argue: If I advise them to sell bonds on the assurance that they are good I am doing so knowing that they must get the consent of the municipalities. They say, that was very well up to 1912, 'but after 1912 conditions differed altogether. The Privy Council, the 'highest court in the land, decided in our favour. They do not tell the public that the decision of the Privy Council is 
based on mere words and not on merits. ,They say that alters the case. But does [DOT] any expert counsel in Ontario or Montreal to whom they went not know that you cannot find out a gross error in legislation like this as a result of getting a decision of the Privy Council and have it rest at that and the whole thing put to sleep? No. The municipalities at once become alert, and every practical man knows that the fight only begins with the Privy Council's decision. They must have known and it was not contradicted, that the very next year, after 1912, the city council of Toronto through Mr. Geary sent down a memorandum.calling for this very amendment, or one in practically the same terms. So the question has ,been before Parliament since the session .of 1913. Every corporation lawyer and .every bondholder must have known that this was a matter of most acute controversy and that it was not going to be allowed to pass simply because Parliament had been defeated of its will by reason of the inefficiency of a law clerk. Therefore, I do not think they are entitled to use that .word " vested rights " with the unction with which they attempt to use it. I admit that there is a strong argument that no one wants to interfere with vested rights, because, in the first place, we are a borrowing nation and if we announce that we are going to interfere with vested rights it' will interfere with our credit, a thing which we do not desire and we want to do the honest thing; we do not want to interfere with rights that have once been given. But vested rights mean rights that have been earned and interference with vested rights means legislation passed for an improper and dishonest purpose. If it is legislation passed only to right a wrong which has been inadvertently done, there is no interference with vested rights. In the Committee we-particularly the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Tweedie) -endeavoured to find out-what it ought to have been very easy to find out-where these bonds went. We had general statements made to the effect that they went ;c France, America, Britain and Canada. I venture to say that most of them were sold in Canada and that the persons who bought them were the same crowd that is in these amalgamated companies. I may be mistaken as to that but I have as anuoh right to suppose and to suggest that as they have to assert the other thing because they did not show where the bonds had gone which they could very easily have done as the records would disclose it.

We had the benefit of the views of ail eminent counsel from the city of New York.
It was a great pleasure to hear him because he is not only a charming speaker but lie is a very clever and highly intellectual man. That was Mr. James Beck and Mr. Beck said that he represented some bond company in the state of Wisconsin but he did not say the amount of bonds that they owned, nor did he say who they were. We were without definite information as to whether any body was fooled or misled in parting with his money by reason of this fortuitous end to the litigation in the Privy Council. I am inclined to think that that is not the real trouble but that is the best argument to use with the ordinary member of Parliament. Every one of us hesitates to vote for anything that interferes with vested rights and a great deal has been said in the las't year or two- about doing anything that will interfere with the credit of Canada. This eminent counsel from New York undertook vo give us a lesson ;n commercial and legislative honesty. While he could give us lectures on commercial ethics, he confined his remarks to the bondholders and utterly ignored a discussion of what would be thought in his country of * making a definite legislative bargain and then trying to repudiate it the moment they saw a little law in their favour. He confined his remarks absolutely to the poor, belated bondholders but if you are going to drag in the morality of the case then I say that it ill becomes any company or amalgamation . of interlocking companies, to charge interference with vested rights or legislative immorality when they themselves are actually undertaking to sell to the public a security which they know is not the one that they got from Parliament because the clause which was put in was put in to protect a certain interest and put in at its behest.
Now, we must answer the great question: "What is the most important thing for us legislators to do under the circumstances? Is this a case which will hurt vested interests and interfere with the credit of Canada? Is'it more important to say: " Walk slowly and safely; it is far better to let it go rather than to have it said in other countries that we had changed our legislation?" Is that to be our sole object, or is it more important to try to protect certain rights and interests? Twenty-five years ago a well-defined movement took place in this country and was brought to the attention of this Parliament. Public opinion demanded an assurance that groups of capitalists and exploiters would be prevented from using the streets of municipalities without the consent of those municipalities. Parliament gave that assurance. Are we now to say that we will break faith with the people in every little municipality in the country who have no time to come down to Parliament to present their case, because it is alleged by this corporation that they have a decision from the Privy Council in their favour, that this is the highest court in the land, and that therefore we must accept the situation? Does any member suppose that when he goes back to his little town, he is going to be able to make an argument of that kind to the people on the streets? His constituents would say to him: Are you going, by legislation, to do a thing of that kind; are you going to set up any such man of straw as that and to say that, because your law clerk misdrew your enactment you have not the power to re-enact it in order to carry out what we sent you to Parliament to do? That must be so. That is not- only the argument that will be heard in Ontario, where these industries are being carried on, but that is the argument in every province in this Dominion. We made a distinct bargain with our people. You have on the one side the public unprotected except by more or less insignificant associations on the one side, you have the monetary interests on the other side, which is disadvantageous to the public interest. It is for us to say what we are going to do. Is it more important to break the bargain which we are said to have made, or to try and amend the bargain which we really made with these corporate interests? To me the question has but one answer, and it is that we must act as the representatives of the public, not as the representatives of the corporate interests, re-enact what we did in 1902, and put this matter really in the same position that it was in when it left this House in 1917.
Now, I come to the amendment. Referring to the present clause as adopted by the Senate, subsection 5, it is apparent that the Senate has brought in a cleverly drawn provision. Subsection 5 says:
Any specific powers inconsistent with the provisions of this section-

That is cut out as regards the Toronto Niagara Power Company. But here they have a sort of parenthesis and they pretend to give the municipalities some rights. They say:
-but if any municipality complain to the Board-
That is the Railway Board.

Now it is perfectly obvious that these words " oppressively, or in bad faith " seem to give some rights to the municipality. In reality they do not give one particle of right, because the mere fact of putting a pole on a street, or putting it on both sides of the street, or putting it at a certain height, is something that is not done oppressively, and is certainly not done in bad faith. It is done in pursuance of the rights conferred by the charter, and such a thing could not possibly be said to be done in bad faith or oppressively. Therefore, if a particular municipality claims that the poles are crooked, or that they are so low as to interfere with firemen getting to a fire, that the poles were not painted, that they were not put down on a proper foundation and might fall, or that they were put down without the previous consent of the municipality's engineer-if any of these things are said and the municipality goes to the Railway Board with the request " We want an appeal from this ?" the Railway Board would say, first of all, " You. have got to show that these things were done oppressively or in bad faith." The municipality could not do so, because there would be no oppression and there would be no bad faith, and so these words amount to nothing, and should be cut out. They seem to be in favour of the municipalities, and I dare say the hope was entertained that municipalities that were not alert might accept them; but municipalities that are alert will not accept something that means nothing. Therefore we want these words out.
I move:

To amend clause 374 by striking out subclause 5 thereof and replacing same by the following:
" (5) The provisions of the last preceding sub-section shall apply to and restrict the powers of any company heretofore incorporated by Special Act, or other authority of the Parliament of Canada, notwithstanding that such provisions may he inconsistent with the-provisions of such Special Act or other authority, and notwithstanding the provisions of Section three of this Act.
(6) If any company heretofore incorporated by Special Act or other authority of the Parliament of Canada has acquired, or shall acquire assets or any part thereof, or the right to the possession or use of the assets or any part thereof, of any company or person operating a system for the distribution of light, heat, power or electricity, in any town, city, village, or township, then in every such case the company so acquiring such assets shall carry out with the municipality all the obligations, in respect to the said assets whether arising under contract or in any other manner, of the company from which the said assets have been or shall be acquired."
The municipalities do not wish to give up any right they now have. That is natural, and the law since 1903 is that while a trunk line can be shoved through a municipality in the case of a transmission line, application must first of all be made for the municipality's consent, and if that consent is withheld the company can go to the Railway Board. But if this power company wants to sell electricity they cannot do it at all without the consent of the city or town, and there is no appeal to the Railway Board. We want to retain, and adhere to, the rights we have had since 1903. Let it be remembered, however, that the rights we had in 1902, under This charter, were that there was no appeal to the Railway Board at all either in case of power transmission or power selling by the company. In 1903 the Railway Act was passed, and now if the company wants the right to go into any municipality, and if the local authorities will not consent, there is the right of appeal to the Board; but so far as selling electricity in a municipality is concerned, we still want the right to say no. That is a right which we have enjoyed all these years. For the reasons which I have given-and I have taken too much time in my statement, not knowing we were going to have a temperature of ninety-four in the shade when I prepared my memoranda on the subject-
I leave the matter to the decision of the committee, hoping that they will rule in favour of the municipalities.

I have listened to the lengthy statement of the hon. gentleman with a feeling of appreciation for the tre-

mendous amount of labour that he must have undergone in preparing his lengthy and technical argument on this subject. 1 feel somewhat modest in daring to raise my voice on the subject at all, in view of the oft-repeated references to "the simplicity of the average layman.'' Fortunately, or unfortunately, I do not happen to be a lawyer, and therefore I suppose, as a "layman" I am to be regarded as totally incapacitated from contributing anything to the discussion of this matter. However, as one who has followed the development of this question during the last two or three months with a great deal of interest and detailed attention, I wish briefly
5 p.m. to state my views in regard to it and my reasons for casting my vote in the way I intend to do when the time comes.
At the outset I desire to resent, and resent very strongly, the inference that any one who ventures to,differ from a gentleman who is advocating what he chooses to call public rights is thereby a special pleader for moneyed interests and corporations. We have heard altogether too much of that sort of argument. As far as I am concerned my record is very clear along those lines; but there is an element of fair dealing and of common sense in all questions, and I claim the right to express my opinions without being subjected to such an aspersion. What we are asked to do is to introduce into a general Act which might be termed the most important civil statute we have on the statute books of Canada, the Railway Act, applying to all railways and to all telephone and telegraph companies, a special provision to deal with an alleged improvident power given to a company some fifteen years ago, thus enabling us' by special language introduced into the general Act to remedy what is alleged to be a wrong.

Will the hon. gentleman
kindly summarize for the benefit of those of us who were not able to be present at the sittings of the special committee just what the points in dispute are between the city of Toronto and the power company?
If my hon. friend has followed the argument-
I could not follow the argument of the hon. member for Parkdale, and I have not yet learned what is the crucial point in dispute.

It was my intention to keep away from private disputes and not to be led into a discussion of them. The
dispute in this case is between the city of Toronto and the Toronto, Niagara Power Company, and allied companies. The point I wish to make is that this Parliament is not concerned with a private dispute. It is now making a law which is applicable to all railway, power, telephone and telegraph companies, and therefore-
I must be permitted to take exception to that statement right from the start. This is not a dispute between the city of Toronto-
