I was saying that I was not going to discuss the question of any private rights, or any private disputes. I was going on to state that we are now passing legislation dealing with all companies of the character mentioned. Now we are asked-I am sure the laboured arguments of my hon. friend from Parkdale will permit me at least to make this reference without interruption-to introduce a provision to remedy an alleged wrong perpetrated in the Act of the Toronto, Niagara Power Company. What are the facts, as far as the framing of the Act we are now dealing with is concerned? The facts are that the disputed case was carried through the courts, the proper place to deal with it. It was dealt with in the court of Chancellor Boyd, who gave a certain decision which I am not going to discuss. On appeal to the Ontario Appellate Court that decision was reversed. An appeal was then taken to the Privy Council, which sustained the ruling of the trial judge. As far as I am concerned I take this stand on the merits of the case: the judgment of the trial judge and the Privy Council is sufficient for me.
The next point I wish to make is that for the past two months at least a special committee of this House sat and heard hour after hour and day after day an exhaustive discussion by the most learned counsel in Canada on behalf of both sides in relation to this case. After hearing them at great length the Committee came to a given decision which decision is contained in the reported Bill at present upon the table of the House. Now, Mr. Chairman, the question is brought up in this Committee-and I admit, it is perfectly proper to do so,- and we are asked to go through that whole process again of arguing this particular point.

If it is the intention of this Parliament to review powers given years ago in a special Act, it ought to be done only after an expert investigation has been held. Then, with the report following such expert investigation in the hands of the members, we should deal with the Aict that it is alleged gave these improvident powers. I wish particularly to emphasize that point. I will repeat it in a slightly different form. If an improvident power was given to the Toronto and Niagara Power Company, and if by virtue of that power they are interfering with municipal rights wrongfully or oppressively or contrary to public interest, - then I claim, Sir, that the way to remedy the evil is by special Act of Parliament limiting or amending or changng or restricting such power. I think I am on sound and safe ground when I make that statement. I do not think it is wise to attempt to deal with the matter as is proposed by the amendment.
The hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Mowat) used an illustration as an argument for sustaining his process. He argued at great length that the Bell Telephone case is analogous to this case. But I would suggest to him, Mr. Chairman, that the Act of the Bell Telephone Company was a private Act, it was an amendment to their original statute, and that is exactly what I am asking this Committee to consider at this moment. The hon. member for Parkdale has provided me with the strongest possible argument for the position I am assuming, namely, that it should be by an amendment to the powers contained in the original charter of the company itself, and not in the general Act. And if the procedure regarding the Bell Telephone Company is worthy of the consideration that my hon. friend suggests then we must inevitably come to the conclusion that it is the proper procedure to follow in this case.
I suggest, Sir, and hold that it is a bad precedent to establish to redress an alleged wrong in a special private Act by amending a general Act. My hon. friend suggests that we are granting enlarged powers to the company. We.&re not doing anything of the kind and that ought to be made perfectly clear to the minds of hon. gentlemen Who had not the privilege of sitting on the Special Committee. We are dealing with all companies in a general way in a general Act; which disposes of that argument at once.
Another point my hon. friend laid emphasis on was that the Senate had amended the Bill we had sent to them. I would re-

mind him that this is a new Bill entirely. True, a similar Bill was before the House in 1917; but that has no relation whatever to this particular Bill. This is the Bill we are dealing with, and we are dealing with it on its merits.
The amendment of my hon. hon. friend reads in this wTay:
The provisions of the last preceding subsection shall apply to and restrict the powers of any company heretofore incorporated by Special Act or other authority of the Parliament of Canada, notwithstanding that such provisions may he inconsistent with the provisions of such Special Act or other authority,
And further, and I wish the Committee to particularly mark this point-
-and notwithstanding the provisions of section 3 of this Act.
Bead section 4 in connection with it.

Section 3 of this general Act-which we have already adopted, by the way-is in this form:
where the provision's of this Act and of any Special Act passed by the Parliament of Canada relate to the same subject-matter the provisions of the Special Act shall, in so far as is necessary to give effect to such Special Act, be taken to over-ride the provisions of this Act.
We are asked to introduce into the Bill another clause which says that notwithstanding that clause we shall disregard the powers given in the special Act. In other words, iii one clause we assert a certain principle, and in another clause we reverse that principle. I submit that that is a very unwise proceeding.
It should also be borne in mind that we do not know what other Acts will be affected. We say in this proffered amendment that it shall apply to all special Acts. During the past fifty years, or since Confederation, hundreds of bona fide Acts have been passed granting powers to telephone companies, electric power companies, telegraph companies, and such like, and yet this committee is asked-and I wish the committee to give this special consideration -to adopt a clause which will disregard all the powers given to private companies up to the present time. And we are asked to disregard them without knowing what powers we are disregarding. I submit that if we are to be consistent at all, if we are-going to amend powers given in private Acts, we ought to have at least some knowledge of the Acts we are amending and the-powers we are restricting.
I have not the statutes before me, but I will illustrate the point by referring to it

couple of companies that I am familiar with. We have in the city of Vancouver a harbour commission incorporated by a special Act of this Parliament. That Act gives to the commission power to bring electricity into the city of Vancouver for the service of power to the harbour, and in the near future the commission are expecting to exercise that power. Now we are asking that that commission shall not have the Tight to exercise that power, although it was given to them in perfect good faith six years ago. In other words, we are asked to take away or amend or restrict that power as given by the special Act. Then I refer to two large companies we have in British Columbia carrying on street railway and electric power enterprises. These two companies are incorporated by special Acts of Parliament. I do not know of any complaint that they have exercised their powers unwisely, unjustly or without due consideration of public rights. As far as I am aware, except for a few local disputes which must necessarily occur, the Western Canada Power Company and the British Columbia Electric Railway Company are both acting in a fairly harmonious manner with the municipalities which they serve, and yet we are asking this Parliament to restrict the powers given to those companies so that they will be subject absolutely to the municipalities.
What powers will be restricted?

As I said a moment ago, I cannot cite the powers. I am merely giving the case of these two companies, of which I have personal knowledge; there must be seventy-five or a hundred other such companies in Canada. Without examining the charters of these companies, should we unreasonably and unduly restrict any powers they may have?

Can my hon. friend name one single provision in the charter of the Western Canada Power Company, or of the British Columbia Electric Railway Company, which will be restricted by this proposed amendment?

In his question, my hon. friend provides the answer. The House is not cognizant at this time of what powers these many companies have; nor can they be without examining each charter-which I am sure I do not propose to do, and I am sure members of the committee do not propose to do.

Can my hon. friend name one single provision in the charters of these
companies which will be restricted or affected by this legislation?

I cannot speak from memory in regard to any one. I did cite the case-had my hon. friend chosen to listen, he would have heard me mention it -of the Vancouver Harbour Commissioners, who are empowered to bring in and distribute power to their harbour works. As they have, for instance, reclaimed areas where they rent or lease lands for factory purposes, and so on, this right is a very important one. Under this amendment, the 'Vancouver Harbour Commissioners would be made absolutely subject to municipal control. I am not saying for a moment that the Vancouver Harbour Commissioners intend or desire to do anything against the interests of the municipalities. But my hon. friend is drawing me entirely away from the point which I wish to make. We are asked ignorantly to restrict-I will put it that way -the powers of private companies by this amendment. Such legislation I allege to be very wrong and very poor, and a danger-our precedent for us to set up in this House.
I wish very briefly to direct the attention of the Committee to that portion of the clause which we are asked to delete. The Committee must get this point into its mind: We are not, under the Bill as it stands, depriving Parliament of any power it may wish to exercise regarding the Toronto and Niagara Power Company. Any time we choose to do so, we can amend that charter; we can do anything we choose with it. We are asked to delete subsection f>
of section 374, the clause which protects the public in what I consider to be a very reasonable manner. It provides that if a company incorporated under the authority of Parliament exercises its powers oppressively or in bad faith, the Board of Railway Commissioners may hear any complaint in that regard and, if it sees fit, super vise the exercise of those powers. The member for Parkdale (Mr. Mowat) contended that in this clause we were using language which made it impossible to deal with the problem. He said that if a municipality went before the Railway Board, complained that this company was exercising its powers unreasonably and asked that its powers he restricted, the Board would insist upon some hair-splitting evidence or proof of oppressiveness. Now, the record of the Board of Railway Commissioners ever since its organization is before this country; it stands out as the one court in the land which ignores matters of hair-splitting evidence and the like. The

farmer, the worker, the private citizen may appear before the Boar.d and get a hearing as good as, if not preferable to, that which he could get before the highest council in the land. I have been before the Railway Board many times, and I know that they particularly care for the interests of municipalities. Municipalities which make representations to the Board receive the most courteous and sympathetic attention. That .is the record of the Board; that is what it is there for. It is not a court of law; it is a court of equity, a court created to protect the public interest, to administer this Act, and to see that its provisions are properly observed. What provision could be fairer than that if a company clothed with certain powers exercises them in any sense oppressively, the municipality-in fact, any person-may bring the matter before the Board of Railway Commissioners? The section provides that the Board may, if it sees fit, " supervise the exercise of such powers ". What does " supervise " mean? It means, direct exactly how a thing shall be done. Our legal friends who have such a profound contempt for the laymen of this House may advance technical arguments with regard to the meaning of words, but every experienced member of the House knows that the Railway Board acts fairly in these matters.
So that there are two points that I particularly wish to make:	First, it is bad
legislation to introduce into a general Act a remedy for an alleged wrong committed by a private company. If a case has been made and a remedy is required, that remedy should be provided by special Act and by amendment of the charter of the company. Second, I submit that the clause as it now stands affords adequate protection to municipalities, to private companies and to private citizens, by enabling this easy appeal to the Railway Board.
I resent the suggestion that any member who dares to raise his voice in opposition to a peculiar view held by our friends from Toronto on this question is derelict to his duty to the public. That is an imputation that should not be allowed to pass, because there are men in this House who are loyal and true to the interests of the public besides the hon. members who happen to sit for the great and holy city of Toronto.
For the reasons which I have stated, I propose to support the Bill as it comes from the special Committee appointed to consider this matter.

'Mr. W. D. EULER (Waterloo, North): Although I listened carefully to the address of the member for Parkdale (Mr. Mowat), I could not entirely follow him; despite that fact, I am still in favour of the amendment. While the point taken by the member for Vancouver (Mr. Stevens) may have some value, it seems to me that in its nature it is more academic than practical. I cannot get past the fact that if this clause passes in its present form, the Toronto and Niagara Power Company will continue to have the power to invade the streets of any municipality in Canada-more particularly of any municipality in Ontario-without first obtaining thq consent of the people of that municipality.
I think the mere enunciation of that proposition condemns it. I think it is a monstrous thing that any private company, no matter how it obtained its privileges, should be allowed to erect its poles and string its wires and carry on its other activities on the streets of any municipality without the consent of that municipality having first been obtained. I do not concern myself particularly about the interpretation of the law under which this company is working. The contention is made that if this amendment is carried Parliament will be interfering with vested rights. Surely, if vested rights perpetuate an injustice, it is not to be suggested that Parliament should not legislate in order to remove that injustice. If a law has been passed in days gone by on any subject that does an injustice to any section of the people or to any person, surely it is within the right of this Parliament to enact legislation that will remedy that injustice. Even the interpretation of the law is debatable apparently. The Toronto and Niagara Power Company, as I understand it, received its original charter in 1902 and the debates of that session make it perfectly clear that it was the intention of Parliament that the company should not have the right to go on the streets of municipalities without the consent of those municipalities. The case came before Chancellor JSoyd and was decided in favour of the company. It was then carried to the Appeal Court of Ontario and was decided in favour of the municipalities. The Privy Council reversed that decision, and sustained the decision of Chancellor Boyd.
In passing, might I make this remark, which may not meet with the approval of the House? The President of the Privy Council has repeatedly stated in this House that Canada is now a nation. If that is the

case, I think the time has come when Canadian courts ought to give a final settlement of all disputes that arise in Canada, and cases should not have to be carried to the Privy Council overseas, no matter how fair their lordships may be. It seems to me that a Canadian court, being right on the spot, is in a better position to give a fair interpretation and a fair decision than any other court outside this country to which the case might be referred.
In this particular case, whatever the law may be, if the rights of the municipality are disregarded, this Parliament is the proper body to protect those rights. Toronto is merely a case in point, and 1 am very sorry to say that I believe there are members of this House who are prejudiced because they believe this is simply a case of the city of Toronto versus the Toronto and Niagara Power Company. I believe that unless this clause is amended the company will have the same rights with regard to the streets of any other municipality in the province of Ontario or in the Dominion that it now exercises in the city of Toronto. The company may have no intention of exercising those rights elsewhere, but it is not at all unlikely that it may do so. It may be that the company in the expansion of its business might see fit to go on the streets of Kitchener, Guelph, Stratford or any other municipality which now controls its own streets and has its own distributing system for Hydro-Electric power.
How do the municipalities of Ontario control their o-wn streets? I submit that they are controlled by the Hydro-Electric Commission.

To some extent ihat is true. I am also of the opinion that the powers that are sometimes exercised by the HydroElectric Commission of Ontario are just a little greater than they ought to be, but that is by the way. Unless this clause is amended we shall be subtracting still further from the rights of the municipalities.
If as a result of this amendment being carried certain interests will be prejudiced and the bonds of innocent bondholders may depreciate, I do not think that is a sufficient reason why this Parliament should consent to perpetuate an injustice and a wrong, if the injustice and the wrong exist. While I believe it would be difficult to prove that any such depreciation would occur in the bonds that have been issued by this company, I would go so far as to say that if it can be shown that loss has
been sustained by reason of the fact that a previous Parliament did not properly protect the rights of the municipalities, it would become the duty of this Parliament to assess and. pay the damages incurred rather than perpetuate an injustice that will affect, so far as we know, all the municipalities of the whole Dominion for all timd to come.

This question has improperly been regarded as one that concerns the municipality of Toronto alone. As I understand it, it is a question of vital importance to every municipality throughout the Dominion. While on some occasions I have been accused of standing inordinately for vested rights, I must say that on this occasion I have a perfectly clear conscience in standing for what I conceive to be the rights of the people with regard to municipal control of their streets as against any kind of company that can be chartered by- the Dominion Parliament. This is not a new question, and it is one that has been debated by business men as well as lawyers, but in very much shorter terms. It may be that I have not the understanding of the question that some of our legal friends have. I felt this afternoon as if I were being taken on a long route march, and nearly fell out by the way. I shall endeavour to say what I have to say within fifteen minutes. This company got very special rights which it was not the intention of Parliament, at the time it got them, it should receive. I may be wrong, but.I believe that it was not the intention of Parliament to allow the Toronto and Niagara Power Company to go wherever they liked in the city of Toronto or any other city in Ontario or the Dominion. Otherwise, a private company would have the right to travel all over this country regardless of the wishes of the people and trample upon property that this Bouse, and this Dominion-and I say this advisedly-does not own in the true sense of the term, because I look upon a municipal street as the absolute property of the municipality in which it exists. Municipal rights as against all comers are to be first considered.
Was that done in this case? Not at all. Ti ls company apparently was enabled to ride rough shod over the wishes of the city of Toronto or of any other municipality in which they chose to plant their wires and poles. Now, what we sometimes term vested rights are really, in the final analysis, vested wrongs, and I say that this is absolutely one of those. It is a vested

wrong; for it gave to a company, either wittingly or unwittingly, property which the giver did not own or control. That is my- point. I am trying to make it very clear that in my judgment the Dominion of Canada did not own those streets and had no right to trample upon the wishes of any municipality. The municipality laid out those streets and probably paid for them. It held the deeds of possession from some one giving it the authority to take those streets for .the uses of the municipality, and its uses alone. But it was not so much in this that the Parliament of Canada went astray, as it was to declare an Act to be for the general advantage of Canada while it was in reality an Act for the general disadvantage of the municipality concerned. That is what the Act did. It was an Act for the general disadvantage of the municipality and would have been better to characterize it in such terms than to say that it was for the general advantage of Canada. I know it will be asked in this House: How are you going to build railways if you do not allow them to expropriate the land through which they are going? Well, the railway when it expropriates land has to pay to the last farthing every one whom it ruins. I do not find that this power company did anything of the kind. They are on the streets and purpose to remain there absolutely forevermore against the wishes of the municipality. Not only are they on the streets at present occupied, but they propose to go on further streets and to expand indefinitely for all time to come. I cannot conceive of any Parliament ever contemplating giving such rights as this, to any private company. It has been said, it is true, that this objection has arisen simply because the HydroElectric Power Company is now in the field to distribute power. I do not think for a moment that that is the case. If I thought that that was the only thing at the back of it, I certainly would have nothing to do with it, though I am a hearty supporter of Hydro power. But I do not believe in giving supreme powers of this kind over streets or lanes or, for that matter, over highways in any municipality in the country. I think they should be obtained by proper authority, and in my conception of it, proper authority in this respect is not within the province of this House. Those who want _ to use the streets should go to the municipality that owns the deeds as against all comers, and where this House made the mistake was to declare that this Act was for the general advantage of Canada when, as I contend, it was dis-
tinctly to the general disadvantage of every municipality into which this or any otheT company might , go.

In other words, they must confine themselves to what the municipality is pleased to give them, and not to be 'told by this House that it is to the general advantage of Canada that they should go where they like, consequently choosing the best street in the city, to the great detriment for all time, of every one who uses the street. I was carried away with his eloquence hut he only touched the comer of the situation, and that was that when the 'Government of Canada declared that this was a work for the general advamtge of Canada there was taken away from all 'the municipalities throughout the Dominion the control of their streets, walks and highways. I want to say to< our lay brothers who are as ignorant of the law a*s I am, that I believe they will take a practical view of this matter and say that no private company should he allowed to go on the streets, sidewalks, lands and highways of a municipality against the wishes of that municipality, because this undertaking has been declared by Parliament to be a work for the general advantage of Canada. I am reminded that the municipality has recourse to the Kailway Board. I think it is provided in the Abt that either the company or the municipality may have recourse to the Eailway Board. But if any municipality complains to the Board that any company whether incorporated by Special or other Act or authority of the Parliament of Canada is exercising its powers oppressively or in bad faith the Board may hear such complaint and if it sees fit supervise the exercise of such powers.
That, to my mind, is holding out & very small straw for the municipalities to grasp at. It says that the Eailway Board "may" hear complaints if it sees fit and it "may" exercise some power. But if the Eailway Board does not see it in that light there will be no recourse and there will be nothing to do further than that; it costs money to appeal to Ottawa. If this House does that in the spirit in which it was originally intended, I feel sure that this amendment, or an amendment directed towards the same purpose, should be incorporated in the Bill. I have much pleasure in supporting the hon. member (Mr. Mowat) in the position which he has taken in regard to this question.

I have ^not had the privilege of being on the special committee that dealt With this question, but I have listened with a great deal of interest to the

hon. member for Vancouver (Mr. Stevens), and I must do him the honour and credit of saying that I always thought he was a lawyer. I have, for the years that he has been in this House, followed the hon. member for Vancouver Centre in the discussions in which he has taken part, and although I had no proof of it, I was always led to the conclusion that the hon. member belonged to that learned profession. I must say for his consolation to-day, that he discussed a principle that is well known to and recognized by the courts of the country, and that principle is that there must be a direct, instead of a lateral, attack upon any point. He argued, and I think conclusively, that if there is anything the matter with the charter of this company there should be a direct and immediate limit to the provisions of the charter, and not a lateral attack upon the company. Our courts, up to the Privy Council, have for years recognized the principle that you cannot laterally-that is by some side issue- attack a right which a person may have, but that you must make an attack direct. If that direct attack is made upon the rights of this company to-day you can, if necessary, give the remedy to Toronto or to any other city that has complained of certain conditions. If Toronto, which is particularly before our minds at present, although this condition might apply elsewhere, is complaining that undue powers have 'been given to this Toronto, Niagara Power Company, then it has the right to come before this House and say that this power must be cut out, and it is open to the House to say that that shall be done. But the power having been granted to this company, they had a perfect right to its exercise. The Privy Council held that the company interpreted the Act properly. Chancellor Boyd, a very distinguished judge of Ontario, has said that the company understood the Act properly. Chancellor Boyd held that they understood their rights; the Privy Council also held that they are merely exercising the powers which the Parliament of Canada gave them. We may have made a mistake in granting these powers, but they were properly understood, they were properly exercised, and if they are to be taken away it is for us to see that nobody shall suffer by reason of any mistake having been made.
(Mr. COCKSHUTT: Will my hon. friend say what he thinks in regard to the opinion expressed by our High Court? He mentions Chancellor Boyd and the Privy Council, but

he omits to mention the third party to the judgment.

That does not count; that was wiped out by the Privy Council, and so it is not necessary for me to say anything about it, as it is absolutely ineffective. The Privy Council said the judgment of the Appellate Court was wrong, and they restored the decision of Chancellor Boyd, and it is that decision which we have to -deal with so far as the construction of the law is concerned. I therefore submit that Chancellor Boyd having said those men had properly used their rights, the Privy Council having said so and confirmed Chancellor Boyd's decision, the Senate of Canada having said that the Bill as presented to us is all right and a committee of this House having done what it considered fair and right with this Bill after having given a proper hearing to everybody who wished to come before them, it is rather late for us-who have not heard the facts, and who have not heard counsel except through the very learned and helpful discussion that took place this afternoon-and rather dangerous for us to interfere with the Bill as presented to us after all the consideration which it has received. I would say to my hon. friend from Parkdale (Mr. Mowat) and to those who support him, in the first place, that I think they have slept on their rights, although that should not weigh wTith Parliament. This Act was passed in 1902, giving this company the powers they have been exercising down to the present, and it is only within a recent period that anything has been brought before Parliament in regard to it. I submit, on the principle so well advanced by my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens), that the attacks should be made directly upon the spot where the mistake took place, and that it should not be sought to secure a remedy by a general Act of this kind, which may do far more harm than the remedy which it is hoped to produce, and which may strike a dozen companies that it is not intended to strike. If it is necessary to provide a proper remedy for the city of Toronto against this power company let the matter come straight before Parliament on its own merits, supported by the essential facts, and then Parliament should be able to deal with it. As far as I am concerned, I cannot see that I would be on safe ground in departing from the conclusions which have been reached by the courts which dealt with the matter, as also by the Senate, and by a special committee of this House.

It is not my intention, Mr. Chairman, to go into a detailed argument in regard to this matter; I prefer rather to pursue the course adopted by the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler).
I wish to reply to some extent to the remarks made by the hon. member for Vancouver (Mr. Stevens). As I understood the hon. gentleman, he said that he thought this House should to a great extent be bound by the finding of the Special Committee appointed to consider the Railway Act. If that had been the only finding, there might be some force in his contention. But I would remind him that at a previous session not only did the Railway Committee of this House, but this House itself, pass an amendment to the Railway Act which was much more radical than the amendment introduced by the hon. member for Parkdale.
I am not going to review the history of the legislation; it has been done so often that the subject is now threadbare. But it seems to me that there are only two or three points of importance in connection with the whole matter. In the first place, we must start out with the primary rights not only of the municipalities of the province of Ontario but of the municipalities of the whole Dominion. These rights were granted to the municipalities as a matter of course long before this special Act incorporating this company was ever thought of, and the municipalities should be given first consideration in any decision this House may come to.
I think no hon. gentleman will dispute the fact that the municipalities have always been accorded the privilege of controlling their own streets, their own highways, their own public squares, and their own lanes, and I do not think that any person will wish to gainsay them that right. It is a form of local self-government that is not only good liberalism, but is good government. It seems to me that this special Act passed in 1902 was a direct violation of those municipal rights. The opponents oi this amendment may argue that Parliament has by a special Act given this company the right to interfere with the streets and highways of the municipalities, and that that right should not be restricted. But I think, Sir, it has been abundantly proved

by hon. members who have preceded me that it was far from the intention of Parliament to grant the extraordinary privilege of going upon the streets and roads of the municipalities without their consent. Therefore on that .account alone we are in a position to review the action of Parliament in 1902, and to pass what at this time is practically a declaratory law- which has been done on many occasions by all parliaments within the British Empire -that it was not the intention of Parliament at that time to enact what the company now claims, and that the law is and should be as this amendment tends to make it.
All the arguments not only in the Special Committee but in this House seem to come down to one question-that of vested rights. No one seems to dispute as a general principle the right of the municipalities to control their own streets. The opponents of this amendment say that on account of the decision of the Privy Council in 1911- after this Act had been in force for some time-investors wefe induced to put their money into the bonds of this company, and those affiliated companies, and that on that account we should not now interfere with the rights given by Parliament in 1902. It seems to me that that contention cannot be sustained, and I think that the hon. member for West Calgary completely annihilated it before the Special Committee.
These people came to us with a charter and they say that they have certain rights -rights decided by the Privy Council to be so and so. But they do not tell us, Sir, that in that very charter, which they allege as the foundation of their rights, their bond issue is limited to $1,500,000. I understand that is the fact. It does not seem to me that, because of their having affiliated with the other companies which have larger bond issues, their claim should be allowed that their charter-Magna Charta, as it were, of their rights-shall not be controlled by the limitations embodied in the charter itself.
It seems to me that they cannot claim the piivileges and the rights which their charter appears to give them-although unintentionally-and not at the same time be willing to be bound by the limitations that that charter imposes upon them.
As I understand the matter this company has invested some eight or nine million dollars of its money and therefore it is more than able to take oare of all the bonds that have been issued by the officers against

its assets. Consequently I do not think it lies with the investors to come before this House and say that the vested interests of this company are going to be interfered with by the action of this Parliament if this amendment is passed.. As I see it, they have no further rights beyond the $1,500,000 which is the limit of the company's bonding powers under its charter.
An effort has been made to arouse prejudice. Some people in the lobbies and some hon. gentlemen-probably not intentionally-in the special committee and before this House have, as I see at, tried to induce hon. members to believe that this is a question between the city of Toronto and the Toronto and Niagara Transmission Company. For my own part, speaking on behalf of the many municipalities in the county of Middlesex, I wish to say that this is not a struggle between the city of Toronto, acting in conjunction with the Hydro Electric Commission of Ontario and the said company; but that if this Bill is allowed to stand in its present form the privileges of every municipality, particularly in the western part of the province of Ontario, are in danger.
I am not an intimate or personal friend of *Sir Adam Beck, but I wish to say for him and for his commission that he has done good work in the province. I can speak from the experience of my home town of Strathroy, and I can candidly say that since the Hydro Electric Commission has taken charge of the distribution of electrical energy and electric light in that town the rates have greatly decreased, and I believe that is the experience of every other town in western Ontario.
Without going further into the argument, because I do not think it is necessary, as others better acquainted with the facts and the law will deal with the matter, I just want to say, that for the reasons I have given I am heartily in favour of the amendment

I have made up my mind to support the amendment of the member for Parkdale (Mr. Mowat). I think it is a move in the right direction; and it is in the interests of the people of this country and against the interests of great promoting companies. The organization behind this company are the greatest promoters of franchises that can be found in Canada. Not only do they receive a large number of franchises; they are exploiters as well. Some twenty-eight years ago this company succeeded in get-

ting the franchise of the Toronto Street Railway. Every one is familiar with this company, the Mackenzie & Mann Company; there is no greater promoting or exploiting company in the Dominion. They paid some $2,500,000 to the city of Toronto for that street railway franchise, which is one of the best franchises ever given to a company in this country. Within a year oi two they issued securities to the extent oi about $6,500,000. They then secured the Toronto Electric Light Company. The city was to have the first opportunity oi securing the benefits of the franchise of the Incandescent Light Company, which was operating at that time, but apparently Toronto was asleep at the switch because this promoting company stepped in and acquired a majority of the stock. A short time after that these promoters undertook to secure what was called the Niagara Development Company. That company has a franchise from the provincial government and supplies power to the Toronto Railway Company and to North Toronto. The franchise of two of these companies expires within the next six months. It was Toronto's intention to secure these two or three companies by arbitration, so they gave a year's notice that they intended to take them over. But at a special meeting of the Toronto city council held a few months ago it was decided to cancel that arrangement and to forego the taking over of these franchises; they decided to allow them to continue for another twenty-one years. The city was quite justified in the attitude which it took. When they gave the notice they felt that they were free to purchase these companies at arbitrated value, but they discovered that the Niagara Power Company had a franchise which permitted them to transmit and retail electric power to consumers in Toronto. Why then, should the city undertake to buy, at a possihle cost of eight or nine millions, the companies at present established there, having regard to the fact that if they did they would be subject to such strong competition? I think they were wise in taking the course that they did, leaving themselves free to meet the competition of the Niagara Power Company if that company chose to enter upon a policy of dealing in power, as their franchise entitles them to do.
It was thought in 1902 by Mr. Osier, Mr. Clarke and Mr. Pringle that the municipalities were well protected. They put up a splendid fight, but they discovered, after some appeals had been made to the Privy Council, that instead of getting something
substantial in the interests of the people, they were handed a gold brick. The Toronto Street Railway Company was an excellent company, having regard to its earnings and the value of its stock. But this promoting company was not content to treat the people as they should be treated; they commenced to exploit the revenues and the earnings of the Toronto Railway Company, and there has been continuous litigation in an effort to get some rights for the people. We thought that the agreement which we had with the company in this case was an excellent one. We knew that we had to be extra careful in dealing with this franchise. We had a splendid mayor at the time, Mr. Clarke, who was always prepared to look after the interests of the people, and he assisted in the effort to get a good agreement from that company. We secured what we thought was the best legal talent in Toronto; some $50,000 was spent in the preparation of the agreement; we thought that it would stand any test in our courts or even before the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council. But to our surprise, as soon as this company got the franchise, they watered the stock, started litigation, went to various courts, appealed to the Privy Council, tied up actions there for months-and invariably the city seemed to get the worst of it; there was some legal point that gave the company the advantage over the people. Instead of extending the street railway system into congested and newly developed parts of the city, they continued to operate on the old lines and refused to extend. The result was that the city was forced to spend millions to give accommodation to the people who needed it. There was nothing but a continuous jamming of people into the cars, in order that the promoters might get the largest possible earnings out of the system. Into a car ol a capacity of say one hundred people, two hundred or two hundred and fifty people would be jammed. The way the women and girls of Toronto were jammed into those cars was a shame and a disgrace. It shows what these promoting and exploiting companies will do to take all they can out ol the people and give nothing in return.
It is said that we are hard on these large corporations; that they have vested rights, and that we should be. more sympathetic. Of course they get vested rights, and whenever they get them they begin to exploit them. It is said that in this case $29,000,000 have been invested; that money has been brought here from England, France and United States, to say nothing of what has come from our own country. Well, the

I am going to support the amendment at the request of the city council of New Westminster, who have wired me to support it as a municipal amendment. I understand that this amendment has received the approval of the Union of Canadian. Municipalities. Personally, I am not interested in any dispute between, the companies which have been referred to. As a matter of fact, I do not know their names. I am looking at the question from the viewpoint of the municipalities, and it seems to me the question involved in this amendment is whether or not the rights, of the people as represented by the municipalities shall he superseded by the rights or privileges of the big corporations. I think it is wrong in principle to allow a great corporation, electric or any other kind, to construct poles and wires on the streets of any municipality without the consent of the people of that municipality. It is admitted that such a privilege should not be granted in the future to any company seeking it.
I	take it from the wording of this section that all companies which have not, by their charters obtained special powers permitting them to go on the streets of municipalities without consent, are required to obtain that consent. I think it is quite clear to everyone that a great many of the special powers contained in Acts of Parliament are obtained without the knowledge of Parliament that they are being conferred. Later on to-night, if I have an opportunity to do so, I shall refer to a case which occurred in this particular session of Parliament in which a very important section of this Railway Act was put through the special committee practically without discussion, and put through this Committee as a noncontentious section. It seems to me that where a thing of that kind happens and where the fact is brought to the attention of the House, it is for Parliament to rectify the condition. It is pointed out that when a company has received these special powers and has obtained what are called vested rights, it is unfair to take these rights away and to require them to get consent, as in the case of the city of Toronto, and it is
suggested that the city of Toronto is trying to hold up this particular company. Now,
I think that if this House is shown on a future occasion that the city of Toronto or any other city or municipality is holding up a public corporation, it will very soon pass legislation to meet the situation.

It has been said several times during this debate that this whole trouble which has disturbed and obstructed our legislation for three years, is due to the bungling of legal gentlemen who were entrusted with the drafting of these statutes some years ago. If that be true, then there is some excuse for those of us who are not lawyers but just ordinary laymen who are taking some part in the discussion. I have not been able to follow the whole matter as closely as some gentlemen, and therefore any opinions I have to offer should be expressed with hesitation and some reserve. I think, however, that I have heard enough of the discussion to grasp the real question that is at issue. I was much impressed by the remarks of the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) as to the unfortunate position in which we are placed when we are asked to use the machinery of a very important general Act for the purpose of making an attack upon the chartered rights of a private company. I think that his argument, that if we wanted to attack the rights of that company we should do it directly and squarely, was an excellent one. However, we must deal with the question in the form in which it is now presented to us.
This is really a fight between vested rights and modern views concerning such rights. I am afraid there is a growing lack of that reverence which existed in olden times for vested rights, and on the other hand that there is a tendency to go a little 'too far in the other direction. There is much to be said in favour of the old-fashioned idea that a bargain is a bargain and a contract a contract, and that all who make it should be prepared to stand by it; and I have a great respect for those who still stand firmly on that view. But there is a strong modern contention that even vested rights must at times be challenged and set aside where they seem to be at variance with public interest. In this case the company has a charter the character of which has been discussed very much here to-day, and, I think, in a manner which perhaps is hardly appropriate. It will not profit us to discuss what was the intention of Parliament when that charter was passed. My legal friends know, better

than do we laymen, that the intention of an Act of Parliament must be gathered from the Act itself, and not from what any one says or thinks about it. In this case, the quality of the company's charter was attacked. They have been able to defend it before the Privy Council, and it stands before us now as a contract which the company say should be observed. But the Senate, sedate and conservative body as it is, and our Committee of this House which has confirmed the Senate's view, have come to the conclusion that even vested rights may in some degree be questioned, and so the Senate has endeavoured to propose something that looks like a compromise. The Senate has virtually said to the company:	True, you have these
vested rights and we do not want to take them away from you, for we respect vested rights, and so on, but we want to be assured that you will exercise them with discretion; and so we include in this Bill a clause which says that if the company in any case-take the case of Toronto, which is very much in evidence-if the company shall attempt to exercise these rights oppressively and in bad faith, then there shall be an appeal to the Railway Board.
Bet us dwell on that for a moment. It is a grea,t departure from the old-time doctrine. It means the raising of a question as to these vested rights, and is an admission that, in the modern view of things, even vested rights may be challenged. But if the Senate-I speak of the Senate because the motion was initiated by them, although it is now before us as a report of a Committee of this House- desired to	grant an	appeal tothe Railway	Commission	under	certain conditions, they might very well have made the appeal more effective. I think the form in which the appeal comes to us is better than what is presented to us by the hon. member for Parkdale, whose amendment does not commend itself to my judgment. I would rather have the appeal in the form in which we have it now than accept his amendment. But while I think that the intention of the Senate in that respect was good, I am of the opinion that if they wanted to give an appeal they should make it a more efiective appeal. They say that if the company go into Toronto, say, and dig up the streets and erect poles and create trouble generally, the Toronto City Council may claim that this is acting oppressively and not in good faith, and may raise an issue before the Railway

Commissioners. It seems to me that if that is a good policy, a better one would be to raise the issue before they dig up the streets or put up the poles, before they exercise any powers at all. My suggestion therefore would be, not to deny the rights of the company, but to provide that if they want to exercise those rights within Toronto or any other city they must first make application to the council of the municipality and see if they cannot come to an understanding with them. I have cast my thoughts into the form of a roughly-drafted amendment, which I shall read in order that the Committee may have clearly before it what I am contending. It will not be in order at this moment, but possibly after the motion of my friend from Parkdale is disipo&ed of I may find it convenient to move it. In the meantime I may read it to inform the Committee of what seems to me to be a fairly good solution of the difficulty:
But when any such company desires to exercise its powers on, in, over, or under any street in any city, town, village or township, it shall be subject to the following conditions:
(a)	The company, when intending to so exercise its powers or any of them, shall give notice in writing to the municipality of such intention and shall, with such notice, furnish plans and specifications of the work proposed to be done.
(b)	If within ten days of the giving of such notice the municipality fail to give notice in writing to the company of objections to the proposed operations the company may proceed to carry on the work in accordance with the plans and specifications.
(c)	If within such ten days the municipality propose to the company in writing changes in the said plans and specifications the adoption of which will remove the municipality's objections, the company shall carefully consider such proposed changes and. shall approve them if they are deemed fair and reasonable, and thereupon the company may proceed to carry on the work in accordance with the plans and specifications as thus modified.
(d)	If the company are unable to approve of the changes of plans and specifications proposed by the municipality, the company may appeal to the Board and the Board, after hearing both parties, may make such order as it may deem expedient, having due regard to the rights of the company and to the public interests affected.
The substance of it is that instead of waiting for Toronto to make a complaint, instead of waiting until the company dig up the streets, put up their poles and raise the devil generally, as the first step notice shall be given to the municipality that they intend to do this. It is hardly an application for permission-the company have a right to do it subject to certain conditions-but before they do it, they shall notify the municipality and give the muni-

cipality a chance 'to make representations. They may be able to agree. Failing in that they shall then go to the board. The difference between that and the provision in the Bill is that while in the Bill as it now stands you would first allow action to be taken, putting up the poles, digging up the street, etc., and then go before the Board of Railway Commissioners and ask them to determine whether this action was oppressive or taken in bad faith, you would have the company first go to the municipality and endeavour to come to an understanding. If they failed they would then proceed to bring the matter before the Board of Railway Commissioners.

Mr. Chairman, the very logical remarks of my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queens (Mr. Fielding) emphasizes the importance of the statement made by my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) at the beginning of this debate. That is that an Act referring to what is purely a local matter within one municipality or a number of municipalities ought not to be incorporated in the general Railway Bill of Canada. I think that if my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queens had been on the sub-committee and had followed the debate, as I am quite sure he would have had he been there, he would have different views from those which he presented to-night. It only shows that when you try to provide for a specific case in a general Act you are sure to land in trouble. There is no set of lawyers in the world who can under such conditions draft a scheme which will not mean trouble in the end. I profess to know something about . this question because I was a member of the sub-committee in 1917 which had this matter under consideration, and we spent, I think, five or six weeks over the whole Railway Bill and some days over this particular clause. Also I was here when the matter was discussed in Committee of the Whole House, and while I was in the minority on that occasion still I had very pronounced views on the whole question, and I have the same views to-night. I was a member also Of the subcommittee appointed a few weeks ago to consider the Railway Bill and spent two or three days over this particular case. We had evidence brought by all the parties, and I believe the subcommittee which dealt with this matter had every particle of evidence which it was possible to obtain or necessary to an intelligent decision. Whether or not the majority gave an intelligent decision is a
question for each individual member's opinion. But it certainly is the fact that the vote was more than two to one in favour of the Bill as it came from the Senate. It is so much like an ordinary lawsuit, so much special evidence bearing upon this paint or upon that point, it is such a localized affair, that one would require to have gone through all the phases of the matter to appreciate the whole position.
My hon. friend from Shelburne and Queens has put up to-day practically the proposition I put up two years ago in principle, but I did not get very far until I saw that there were difficulties ahead, that there were lions in the path.. My hon. friend talks about going to a municipality-mind you, I am talking about this particular case; on the general case 1 agree with him at once; I do not think that any corporation should receive the right to go upon the streets and public squares of any municipality without the consent of that municipality; in the light of our experience 1 doubt if there is a man in the House of Commons or the Senate who would advocate that we should give a charter to-day such as was given in 1902. But my hon. friend was discussing this matter from a general standpoint and from the general standpoint he is absolutely logical. He says that before anything is done the corporation should give notice to the municipality of their desires accompanied by plans and specifications of the works and ask if the municipality is prepared to consent; if they do not object in ten days, go on with the work, if they do object, go to the board. But my hon. friend fails to realize and-I say this in no offensive way-fails to understand that a municipality in the province of Ontario has nothing to say about it, absolutely nothing. I know my hon. friend will hardly believe that statement

I think I do.
. Mr. CARVELL: -but I want to read to him the law of Ontario to-day. A municipality has no control over its streets when it comes to the question of erecting poles for the transmission of electricity. By an Act passed in 1914 it is provided .that:
. Notwithstanding- anything in any Act contained a municipal corporation shall not hereafter enter into any agreement with any such company or pass any by-law in relation to any public utility which has been declared to be a work for .the general advantage of Canada, or which is not within the legislative control of Ontario, until the Lieutenant-Governor in (Council approved of such agreement or .by-law, and every agreement entered into and by-law

passed in violation of this section shall be utterly void and of no effeot.
Is that Ontario law? Mr. CARVEiLL: That is Ontario law.

My hon. friend will find in the suggestion I offered that there was nothing about making an agreement with the municipal council. What I suggested was that the municipal council should be afforded an opportunity of accepting or of stating their objections. I thought I succeeded in steering clear of the trouble to which my hon. friend refers.
Mr. 'CARVEILL: I do not want to steer clear of it; I want to face it; let us try to face it and see if we can get legislation passed which will be equitable and will meet the situation. There is nothing here about any notice to the municipality, and you have the right to erect poles on any one of their streets without the municipality having anything to say about it.

I do not propose that they shall ask for the right. I say, on the contrary, that the company have the right, but it is a question as to the manner in which they shall exercise it. I do not propose that they shall go to Toronto and ask them for the privilege, but that they shall go to Toronto and say: We have the privilege; we come to say that we wiH exercise that privilege in the way we think best, but we wiant to afford you an opportunity of filing objections.
Has not the municipality a perfect right to pass a by-law? But the opinion of the minister is that the Government of Ontario would never consent to its enforcement.

I will read that over again. First, I will answer my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's and then my hon. friend from Centre Toronto (Mr. Bristol). This subsection that I have read was framed by a man who evidently knew what he was doing, because they do not apply this to all corporations, but to corporations which have been declared works for the general advantage of Canada-which means the Toronto Niagara Power company and allied interests. It uses the word " agreement.'1 If the suggestion of my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queen's were carried out, if an application were made to the municipality and if the company said: We want to erect these poles and build this line under certain conditions; and if no objections were made, that would be an agreement. I think it comes within the purview fMr. Carved]
of the amendment and therefore I would add here -to my former statement that the municipality is absolutely powerless. Now, to answer the hon. member for Centre Toronto, this law specially declares that:-
-and every agreement entered into and' bylaw passed in violation of this section shall he utterly void and of no effect.
That is the point I make: They can pass ithis by-law, but it is no good without the sanction of the provincial government.

Exactly, it is only a scrap of paper, and the whole legislation was framed in order to prevent the Toronto and Niagara Power Company from doing business. I want now to discuss for a moment or two the general question involved.

Before the minister leaves that subject, there is a point that I do not quite follow. If the company created, or incorporated, by this House is given certain rights in any province of Canada, does the minister think those rights can be taken away by a provincial enactment?

No, but I have no doubt that the province of Ontario is quite right in saying that a contract made by one of its municipalities with this corporation would be void. I think they are right in that and. that is what they have done. They have not said that the Toronto and Niagara Power Company cannot do certain things, but they have said that no municipality can pass a by-law agreeing that anything shall be done by this corporation without its being null and void.
Is not that an indirect wiay of doing the same thng?
It may be, but I believe that under the British North America Act they have those rights; I believe their powers go that far.

Suppose the Toronto and Niagara Company notify the city council of Toronto that they intend to carry on certain work, under certain plans and specifications, and want to know if the council have any objection, and the council say they have no objection, does my hon. friend say that is a by-law?

I think it is, and I will go as far as to say this: If I were representing the province of Ontario, or the Hydro-Electric Commission, I would not hesitate a moment to take the case to the

courts and should expect to get a decision, because they have used the -word "agreement," as well as "by-law." "Every agreement entered into, and by-law passed, in violation of this section shall be utterly void and of no effect." I think my hon. friend will find that the man who drew this section knew what he was doing. He /knew he was aiming especially at the Toronto and Niagara Power Company, and he was determined that that company should not be able to do any business in competition with their own company. Now I have no fault to find with the province of Ontario in its Hydro-Electric proposition.
I agree with my hon. friend from West Middlesex (Mr. Ross) that the Hydro-Electric Commission in Ontario has done a great work, and I believe is destined to do still greater work in the near future. I am somewhat of an admirer of the commission for the way in which they have carried the work on. I do not believe they are get>-ting as cheap power as they think they are, because they have to pay certain taxes; but there is no doubt in the world that the householder is getting cheap electricty. More than that he is getting a sufficient supply in ordinary times, which, after all. is more than the question of price. Therefore I have nothing but kind words for the Hydro-Electric Commission; and if it be 'the wish of the people of Ontario that that commission shall be the only corporation generating, transmitting, and distributing electricity in Ontario, that is their affair also; if they want to adopt that policy I do not think the Parliament of Canada should find any fault with it. But I do lay down this . doctrine: That they have no right to ruthlessly step in and destroy other men's labours and destroy the capital which other men have put into these schemes before the. Hydro-Electric was an entity at all. When we practically got through with the hearing of the evidence before the special committee I asked a series of questions of the gentlemen present. In a sense it was like a series of questions which a judge would propound to a jury in court, but the answers were given by both parties to the dispute. I am going to read to the committee the questions, and the answers, and therefore the committee can accept these as being the facts of the case as produced in the evidence before the special committee: 1 2 * *
1.	Q. When did the Toronto and Niagara, oi subsidiaries, first deliver electricity in Toronto? -A. 1907.
2.	Q. When did the Hydro-Electric Commission first deliver electricity in Toronto?-[DOT]

What company is that?
That is the Hydro Electric Commission, or in other words, the province of Ontario.
Is not that the municipal company in Toronto?

No, it is the Hydro Electric Commission. I did not ask the details, but I presume a company-that is*, the city of Toronto-is working with the HydroElectric Commission in buying electricity and distributing it, but that means a. company in competition with the Toronto and Niagara.
Toronto is a customer of the Hydro Electric Commission?

No. I think foeiore I get through my hon. friend will see that I have some other ideas in the back of my head on the subject besides that.
Mr. MaMASTER: In a memorandum which was distributed among Jhe members in the House the statement is made that when this charter was granted to the Toronto. and Niagara Power Company it was thoroughly understood that the company obtained the right to go into Toronto subject to the approval of the municipality. * would like to hear the minister on that point, as it appears to me to be important.

I was not a member of Parliament at that time, and therefore I have no personal knowledge of the matter. However, from reading Hansard of that day there is no doubt that the matter was discussed, and I think that very many people believed that they would not have the right to invade the streets of any city without the consent of the municipality.
But my hon. friend from Shelburne and Queens (Mr. Fielding) in his usual logical fashion has, I think, answered that question. It is not a question of what he or I or some other member of Parliament- may have thought; Parliament acts as a whole,

and the combined wisdom of the whole Parliament finally incorporates certain ideas into law; and from that day forth it is- a question for the courts to decide what Parliament did intend to do. And t'he Privy Council has said that Parliament intended that the company should have the right to go on the streets of every municipality in the province of Ontario.
The House of Lords decided that all the property of the Presbyterian Church was to go to the "Wee Frees, and legislation 'had to be passed to correct such an absurdity.

My friend is a better authority on that then I am, and therefore I will not be drawn into that discussion,-theology is not my /strong point. When I was interrupted I was stating that it takes three things to make a successful hydro-electric scheme after the parent company was formed-and without the parent company the scheme was never possible because unless 'they had the right to transmit and distribute energy they never would have spent a dollar. Therefore, all the corporations that have been built up around this company were built up 'because of the rights and powers granted to the parent company by Parliament in 1902. They got these three things going and spent about $35,000,000. It is in evidence, and not denied, that there are $29,000,000 worth of bonds now outstanding against- the scheme, and $9,000,000 of those bonds have actually been absorbed by the purchasing public since the decision of the Privy Council i11 1912. I think .it is a fair assumption that the people who bought those bonds since 1912 bought them on the strength of the law as interpreted by the Privy Council-that this company had the right to distribute electricity through the municipali-ies of Ontario or anywhere else that they might he able to go to.
In pursuance of those rights the company built a transmission line from the Falls to the city of Toronto. Then they had a contract with the city of Toronto by. which they were given the right to erect certain poles in the city for the purpose of lighting the streets. The contract extended down to 1915 or 1916-1 have forgotten the actual date. The Privy Council decided that the company had no further right to maintain those poles on the streets of Toronto-that is the Toronto and Niagara syndicate now- because they got the right up to a certain date for the specific purpose of transmitting [DOT] electricity for street lighting, and when that

contract expired the right to maintain the poles expired with it; and that is where the matter stands to-day. It is also a fact that the Toronto Electric Light Company, which is a part of this scheme, has a very extensive underground system in the centre or congested portions of the city.

Is not the question of having overhead wires entirely one for the municipalities? What right have we to interfere? And if the municipality is going to allow the Hydro-Electric to distribute their power in that way, why should we interfere?
Not at all.
Then why make a point of it?

I am pointing out that the city of Toronto have no objection to overhead wires in their streets, 'because, they have allowed the Hydro-Electric to distribute everywhere they want to by an overhead system; but when it comes to a competing company the city say to them: " No, you must not distribute your electricity by overhead wires." As I said before, the Toronto Electric Light Company have a very extensive underground system in the centre of the city, and tlhat underground system is fed by overhead wires, and if this company is not allowed the Tight to use overhead wires in conjunction with their underground system, then that underground system is no good except as junk. Because, they mi^ht have the most elaborate distribution system in. the world, but if they cannot get current to it it is only junk. If this amendment were passed -let there be no misunderstanding about it-the Toronto and Niagara Company cannot maintain a single wire in the city of Toronto, they cannot get a watt of electricity through their underground system, and their underground system becomes absolute junk and is only worth junk value.
I understood the Toronto officials to say they would allow the company to transmit power on the overhead lines to the underground.

My friend is usually
more astute, and it is a confession that I did not expect him to make this evening, because that question was thrashed out in the special committee for hours, and he was there. I framed these questions based upon that very statement of facts:	I
asked:
Q. Does the Hydro-Electric maintain overhead wires for both transmission ant distribution?-A. Yes.
Q. Can the Toronto Electric Eight Company feed its underground system without using overhead lines in the city of Toronto?-A. No.
That was admitted by everybody.
Who answered that?

Mr. Fleming was there
from one side, and Mr. Kilmer from the other.
Mr. Kilmer did not answer in that way.

No objection was taken
to it.

I rather resent that
statement from my friend (Mr. Cahill) and I say so frankly. I am not coming before this Committee to state what are not the facts. As my friend from Perth (Mr. Morphy) tells me, they stated the underground system was scattered over different parts of the city, and it would be a physical impossibility to dig a tunnel from the outskirts of the city to connect with that scattered system. There was no question about the matter at all; everybody admitted the facts were that without the overhead distribution system you could never feed the underground. I would, not come here and misstate the facts. I have been at the bar too long to attempt such misrepresentation.
Let us see the result. My friend says, " Well, but they are going to allow them to distribute overhead." What does the amendment provide? Subsection 5 is as follows :
The provisions of the last preceding subsection shall apply to and restrict the powers of any company heretofore incorporated by special Act or other authority of the Parliament of Canada, notwithstanding that such provisions may be inconsistent with the provisions of such special Act or other authority, and notwithstanding the provisions of section 3 of this Act.
Section 3 provides that if they are not satisfied with the arrangements for distribution, if the conditions imposed are too onerous or unfair, they can apply to the board, Notwithstanding everything, if this amendment passes, then the Toronto and Niagara Company are absolutely barred from getting electricity for their underground system in Toronto. There you have the facts of the case put as plainly and concisely as I am able to express them. It is also admitted that their principal consumers are two corporations in Toronto: first, the Toronto Electric Light Company,

which the city of Toronto have the right to purchase up to the month of November next, but the city has now notified the offl-' cials of the company that they do not intend to purchase the system. If the amendment passes, the Toronto and Niagara Company cannot feed their underground system, and therefore that system is only junk.
It is also admitted that in 1921 the city has the right to take their next greatest customer, that is, the Toronto Kailway Company. You take away from the Toronto and Niagara Power Company the Toronto Railway Company, and you put the Transmission Company where they cannot dispose of their power. What, then, are they going to do with their output? What is the value of their output in Toronto? What is the value of their transmission line? What is the value of their generating plant, if they are not allowed to transmit electricity to the United States? If this amendment passes I have no hesitation in saying that two years from now their bonds would not be worth 50, because the physical assets of the company that would be left to them would not realize more than fifty per cent on the value of the bonds. If the Parliament of Canada is absolutely to commandeer or destroy a corporation such as that, which has been built up on the basis of legislation passed by this Parliament in good faith, then it is for them to say so; but I want to see the members of this House vote to do that before I believe it is possible that the representatives of the people have reached the point where they will confiscate property which represents money invested in good faith at a time when the undertaking seemed very much of' an experiment. I believe I am safe in saying that when this company decided to transmit electricity from Niagara Falls to Toronto it was the longest transmission line in existence in the world-nearly one hundred miles. They were pioneers in what became one of the greatest assets of the civilized world. They got a charter which, I admit, looking backward on it now, is a very favourable one; but they got it in good faith and invested their money in good faith. And if this amendment is adopted, the earning capacity of 'this property is absolutely gone; it can only be sold as junk.
Is the section as it now stands in the Bill just as it was passed in the committee?1

Assuming that the right of the company to go on the streets of Montreal or any other city without the leave of the municipalities be taken away, on what does my hon. friend base the idea that these assets are worth only fifty cents on the dollar?
I thought I made that plain.

They are developing
250,000	horse-power at Niagara Falls now.

We are dealing with a specific case, not with a general law. We have a case which ought not to be here at all, or which, if here at all, ought to be in the form of an amendment to the charter of the Toronto' and Niagara Power Company. But I will go over the ground again. The' Toronto and Niagara Power Company have only two principal consumers of their product, first, the Toronto Street railway, which the city of Toronto will take over two years from now and which will be entirely operated by hydro-electric current;-my hon. friend will agree to that?

Yes, but when they made that contract with the Toronto Railway Company they charged them $45 per horsepower and got the Toronto Railway Company to guarantee their bonds. It was that fact that caused Toronto and the whole of Ontario to look aghast on the whole situation.

My hon. friend is introducing local politics into the matter; I do not propose to drag such considerations into it at all. I do not care what their contract was in Toronto; I am dealing with the facts of the case as revealed in the Committee.
But, pardon me; the franchise of the Toronto Street Railway Company expires in two years, anyway.

I know that; I am not so dense as not to realize all these things. I know that in two years from now they are going to lose the right to sell 'electricity to the Toronto Railway-Company. Toronto has the right to abrogate that contract and take over the Toronto Electric Railway Company.
We should like to have the benefit of the whole of this discussion. We can hear the minister, but we cannot hear the member for Toronto Centre (Mr. Bristol).
