speechtext:
The Minister of Public Works has the floor.

Mr. 'CARVELL: I have no objections whatever to interruptions; I am glad to argue the matter from every possible standpoint. I am not at all afraid of my premises; therefore I welcome any questions the member for Toronto Centre wants to put to me. Now, I will finish my answer to him. In the next place the greatest consumer of current from this company is the Toronto Electric Light Company. The city of Toronto has the right to buy that company out also. That right expires in November of this year and the city have now notified the company that they will not buy them out. I have pointed out that if this amendment carries there is no earthly possibility of the Toronto Electric Light Company getting their current to their underground system, because they cannot maintain one pole in Toronto, and if the'Toronto and Niagara Power Company cannot get current to any part of that system, what earthly good is the Toronto Electric Light Company to them? It is absolutely useless; it is a dead horse to them, and they might as well sell it for ten per cent of what it cost them. I know something about this business; 1 have been in it for fifteen years, and I know what it means if you have a dead line and cannot get electricity to it. All you can do is to sell it as old copper; you can take the expensive switch-boards and sell them at twenty-five cents on the dollar. If the city of Toronto, or whoever the competing powers are, want to be fair, they will say: We will buy you out-and if they will buy them out, that is all right.
Now, I think I have answered my hon. friend. If you take from this company their two principal customers in Toronto you render the whole scheme absolutely useless, unless they are allowed to export electricity to the United States. But what is the position? We have the chairman of the HydroElectric demanding that we prohibit the export of electricity to the United States. Just as sure as this Bill went through, in the next week a demand would come up on behalf of certain people in Ontario that this Government prohibit the exportation to the United States of one watt of electricity generated by this company. If my premises are at all correct, I want the member for Toronto Centre, when he replies to me, as I assume he will, to show me where in the world this company is going to get the money to pay their bonds.
But the amendment goes further than that. The hon. member for Parkdale wants Parliament to say, in substance-it is very doubtful whether it could be said, under
our constitution-that if the Toronto Electric Light Company has sold any part of its plant or assets to the Toronto and Niagara Power Company, the arrangement shall be void. In all my experience in Parliament, extending over a long period here and in New Brunswick, I have never heard a proposal to confiscate moneys put up in good faith, on the faith of legislation granted by Parliament. It may be good morals in Ontario, but I can tell you that in the part of Canada from which I have the honour to come, it would be considered mighty bad morals.
Now, owing to the manner in which we have discussed this thing, I have taken more time than I intended to take, but 1 wanted to lay before the committee the facts of the case as I view them. I hope that the Parliament of Canada will not stultify itself by adopting the amendment proposed by the member for Parkdale. I use the word advisedly; I know it is a strong one, but I have no other word in my vocabulary which correctly interprets my views on this matter. Something else might be done. Something might be done to limit the powers. The company might be limited territorially; they might be allowed only to proceed in certain portions of Canada; I am not so much concerned about that. But to say that the company shall not have the right to continue doing business, shall not have the right to carry on the business which Parliament gave it the right to carry on, is a doctrine which I do not think this Parliament will accept.

I did not have the privilege of hearing this matter discussed before the committee. Provided the rights of the city of Toronto are safeguarded in respect to the use of their streets, is there any special objection to the presence of this company doing business in the city?

I do not want to draw conclusions; I certainly do not want to impute motives, but you must remember that this company has just one competitor, and that is the province of Ontario, and you must remember that this company cannot make a contract with any municipality except with the consent and approval of its competitor. Now if this amendment passes, this company cannot do any business in the city of Toronto because the city of Toronto is its competitor. That is the reason why the city of Toronto will not buy out the Toronto Electric Light Company. We have heard it stated very plainly-I do not know that I can bring a man
3J 04

here as a witness to swear to it-that the city of Toronto have refused to buy out the company because they say: "We can squeeze them out by refusing to feed their underground system, and if they cannot get their underground system fed we will take the company over as a junk proposition."

Does the minister believe that it was the intention of Parliament at that time to grant such wide powers? Does he believe that the company thought when they got this charter that they had a right to go 'on any street in any city in Canada and distribute power?

I can only answer that from the evidence. I believe that Mr. Clarke and Mr. Osier were satisfied that the company did not have the powers which it turned out they had. I think that probably Mr. Pringle and Mr. Cowan were two members of Parliament who at that tinie did not believe the company had the powers which it turns out they had. As to what the rest of Parliament believed I do not know, because the other two hundred and twenty members were silent on the question, and I have no way of going back seventeen years and divining their thoughts. There was no secret about it, because the very year Mr. Urquhart, mayor of Toronto, brought the matter to the attention of the city council and pointed out that the company had acquired the exact powers which the Privy Council says they got. That was told in the city council in 1903, and yet the city allowed this company to occupy their streets and do practically what they had a mind to with them for years and years, and it was not until 1914 or 1916, I believe, that the city raised a protest. So, no matter what may have been the views of four or five members of Parliament, the people of Toronto knew what powers this company had, and allowed them to exercise them without protest for ten or twelve years.
The minister stated that the city of Toronto wanted to squeeze out this company. Is it not true that the city of Toronto offered to buy out the company at 135?

I have been told that
that is true, and that the stock was then worth about 160 and the company refused to sell. This is only hearsay, and I have no way of proving it. It was not mentioned in the sub-committee. No evidence was

given to that effect; I am only giving hearsay.

In other words, the Lords of the Privy Council, said, in the interpretation of this Act, that they could not read nor consider anything that might have been done or said when the matter was before this House, but had to determine the Act purely within the four corners of the statute. The Minister of Public Works, if I am correctly advised',-at may be that I am not-is wrong in his contention that 'from 1902 to 1911 this company went on and exercised its rights ruthlessly and without regard for the municipalities. If I am correctly informed, this company bought its right of way for its transmission line from Niagara to Toronto and did not force itself through municipalities but worked itself along as a transmission line by purchase or with the consent of the municipalities through which it passed.

Will the hon. member
pardon me. I do not think I said " ruthlessly," and certainly I did not intend to say so. I said they went on and developed under the powers given them by Parliament. I have never heard that they have done anything but carry on a straight business proposition, and I would be the last man to say that they ruthlessly invaded any rights. I did not say so.
As I understand the minister now he says the company went on and exercised its statutory rights.
That is right.

Let us see how they exercised those rights. From 1902 to 1911 they did not presume to erect poles or wires either for transmission or distribution in any municipality without the consent of the municipality. But in 1911 there was a change of policy. In that year they entered the streets of a suburban district of Toronto known as North Toronto, and without obtaining the consent of that municipality, proceeded to erect poles and wires for the purpose at least of transmission, and, I think, also of distribution. An action was launched by the town of North Toronto and was first heard by Mr. Justice Boyd of the Supreme Court of Ontario who gave a decision to the effect that they had a right to erect those poles and wires provided they did not incommode the people of that municipality. But in so far as the reading of that ease leads one to a conclusion, the attention of the Chancellor was not directed to the fact that section 90 of the Railway Act was incorporated in the Act of the Toronto and Niagara Power Company. From

the decision of the Chancellor an appeal was taken to the Court of Appeal by the municipality of North Toronto, and the Court of Appeal unanimously was of the opinion that the Toronto and Niagara Power Company had not the right to erect poles and wires in that or any other municipality without obtaining the consent of the municipality. They were of the opinion that section 90, incorporated in the act of incorporation of the Toronto and Niagara Power Company by section 21 of that Act, was not inconsistent with the powers given by sections 12 and 13, but simply qualified those sections, and that the consent of the municipality had to be obtained before poles or wires either for transmission or distribution could be erected. An appeal was then taken by the Toronto and Niagara Power Company to the Privy Council, with the result that the Privy Council, relying on the principle of law which I enunciated a few moments ago, that they could not go outside the four corners of the statute, reached the conclusion and gave a decision that section 90 had no application to the charter of the Toronto and Niagara Power Company, and for the first time the residents of the province of Ontario, to say nothing of the people of Canada, woke up to the fact that the Toronto and Niagara Power Company had a right that enabled them 'to go on the streets of any municipality either for the purpose of transmission or for the purpose of distribution, and that there was no municipal power in Canada that could say them nay. Not only had they this right for a limited period of time, but they had a perpetual charter extending not only in the province of Ontario but from the Atlantic to the Pacific. Now, let us understand exactly what the rights of this company are as claimed to-day and what rights we, as members of this House, are asked to confer by passing the legislation as it comes to us from the Senate. Hon. gentlemen present in this House to-night are being asked to say that the Toronto and Niagara Power Company have the right to erect distribution poles and wires in any municipality in Canada without getting the consent of that municipality. Now, Sir, had it not been that representations were made to the Committee in 1902 and again to the House in the isame year to the effect that these rights should not be exercised except with the consent of the municipality, I am inclined to the opinion that I would find myself in the same quandary in which the Minister of Public Works is placed to-night. The difference between us lies in this: He does not view the matter in such a way as

to feel justified in going beyond the four corners of the Act; I view the matter in a broader way, or perhaps I should say, in a more extended way, I think that we as a high court of Parliament have the right to go beyond the Act and to study and give consideration to, and to have our decision influenced by, the conditions and representations under which that Act was obtained. I say that it is a sound principle of law that if A represents as a fact to B something upon which B relies as a fact and acts thereon, A is estopped from contending as to the truth of the representations made. Applying that principle of law to the charter that is before the Committee to-night for consideration indirectly, I say that in my opinion this House has the right to say that if the promoters of this legislation in 1902 represented to this Parliament that they -were only getting a limited franchise, when they either knew they were getting a more extended franchise or were ignorant of the fact that they were getting a more extended franchise, we as a House of Commons have the right to say: You are bound by the representations you made in 1902 and have no greater privileges and rights than you protested and led the House of Commons to believe you had. It is on that principle that the Minister of Public Works and I differ. He takes-if I may use the expression without being considered offensive-the narrow legalistic position that might be taken by a judge. On the other hand, I take what I consider to be the more extended position, that as a member of Parliament I have the right to review the conditions under which any legislation is obtained. It is a question on which men of different minds may reach different conclusions, and different conclusions may be honestly reached. But in my judgment there is no anomaly in this Parliament saying, by the legislation that is proposed by the hon. member for Toronto, we are going to bind this company to the same principles that they were prepared to accept in 1902.

But is not that what was attempted to be done in 1902 when section 90 of the General Railway Act was incorporated into a private Act? All that is being asked here to-night is that section 374, which is, if I may use the figure, the legitimate descendant of section 90, shall be s'o amended

Any specific powers inconsistent with the provisions of this section and conferred on any company by any special or other Act or authority of the Parliament of Canada or of any province, shall not be affected by the provisions of this section, but if any municipality complains to the Board that any company, whether incorporated by special or other act or authority of the Parliament of Canada, is exercising its powers oppressively or in bad faith, the Board1 may hear such complaint, and, if it sees fit^, supervise the exercise of such powers.
Now the Railway Commission may be animated with the best intentions in the world, .buit, as the bon. gentleman knows, their .power in respect of any matter that comes before them for consideration are determined and limited by the language that gives them that power. Indeed the language of subsection 5, as it appears in the Act simply gives the Railway Commission .power to supervise when the powers are oppressively or in bad faith exercised. Now that practically means nothing; they can simply .supervise, they cannot prohibit. I would think that the extent that would permit them to go would be thus far: If the Toronto and Niagara Power Company determined that they would erect a very unsightly and unseemly class of poles on a certain thoroughfare through which the use of that street would be greatly encumbered and the people greatly irritated, and dn such event all the Railway Commission could say would be: "You must use a different style

of poles and you must locate them somewhat differently on the street I do not believe the Railway Commission would have the right to say to the company, " You shall not go through that municipality." The amendment means that those of us who are supporting it desire the principle incorporated in the Railway Act that no company shali have the right, no matter whether they have special powers or otherwise, to go through the streets of any municipality for the purpose of distributing electricity without the consent of that municipality.

Now, in regard to 'the matter of transmission, the principle is accepted and recognized that a transmission line may be built through a municipality with its consent; but if the municipality is not willing that that transmission line shall be built then there shall be an appeal to the Railway Commission and the decision of the commission shall he final. Now hon. gentlemen ask me why the occasion for the difference? Why do you make one law as to transmission and another law as to distribution? The difference dn principle is this: It is absolutely essential

The Toronto and Niagara Power Company was incorporated in 1902. In 1903, Messrs. Mackenzie, Nicholls and Pel'latt made an agreement with the Ontario Victoria Park Commission for the right to develop a certain number of horse-power. speakeroldname: Hon. J. D. REID (Minister of Railways):
speechtext:
I do not like to give a silent vote on this important matter; therefore I would like to say a few words before the vote is taken, this Bill has been before the committee for several weeks-yes, it has been before the
House for some three years. It is in the interest of the country that the Bill should go thiuugh the House during the present session, and I hope that the House will arrive at some decision which will enable u- to pass the Bill. I think every member of the House wishes to do what is fair and right not only with the municipality, but with this company or any other company that has been incorporated by this or any other Parliament. Some hon. members have suggested that if this charter was brought before the House to-day for approval it would not pass; that we would not grant any such conditions as were granted when this charter was given. But Parliament has granted many charters in the past that would not be granted to-day.	I	can refer to one.	Anumber	of	years ago	the	House	of
Commons granted a charter to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company; if that charter was before the House to-day, there is no doubt that it would not pass now in the form in which it passed then. In connection with the charters which were granted in those times certain vested interests have arisen, and I think we should look at the situation in the light of all the circumstances connected with the charter.
So far as I am concerned, I feel this way. The rights of municipalities should be protected if any danger threatens them. It has been stated by many that the rights of municipalities are in danger in connection with this charter. But I wish to point out that since this charter was granted the Ontario Government has passed an Act which has changed the whole condition of affairs for the municipalities. When the charter was granted the municipalities had, in their own right, the power to allow this or any other company to enter that municipality on the basis of a by-law or agreement. But in 1914 Ontario passed an Act, which has -been mentioned this afternoon,' taking out of the hands of the municipalities the right that they had at that time to allow this or any other company to enter those municipalities. If the Bill passes there is no doufet that this company or any other company can enter into any municipality without the consent of that municipality.
That may be all right in many o-theT parts of the Dominion, but -so far as the province of Ontario is concerned the consent of the Ontario Government has to be obtained. That being the case this company -cannot do any business between the city of Toronto and its power plant, if a

municipality should refuse to allow it to pass through, and if the company is prevented 'from transmitting power in that way it must go on the scrap heap. I think it is quite proper to protect the interests cf the municipalities, but we should also do something to protect the money that lias been invested in- this company.
This legislation, has been before the House for several years. I will tell the Committee what I think should have been done some years ago, and what should be done yet. The province of Ontario practically decided that power would be supplied to the people of the province by the Ontario Government. That policy has turned out to be a good thing for the people of the province; we all agree that the Hydro-Electric 'Commission has done good work. But when they decide to supply all the power to the people of the province of Ontario, I think they should take over the power plants in the province of Ontario and not make them junk, which would involve a loss of the money invested in those plants. It would only be fair for the Ontario Government to tell these power companies at Niagara Falls that they were going to take over these plants at a price fixed by arbitration; then get the arbitrators to determine the value, and let the Ontario Government take over the plants and have the power for the people of the province. The Toronto and Niagara Power Company is not the only one at Niagara Falls developing power. There is another company thers developing 100,000 horsepower, all of which will be required by the people of the province. Both are up-to-date plants, they have their transmission lines, and I cannot understand why the province of Ontario does not adopt that policy, with respect to the plants not only at Niagara Falls but also at other places where electric plants- owned by companies are in operation. I think men could be found to arbitrate on the value of these plants and decide what was a fair price. I am sure the people of the province of Ontario would be willing to do what was fair with regard to this or any other company in the province that might be arbitrated upon.
But that does not seem to be their policy, and therefore we in this House are placed in this position. Here we have been for three long years trying to enact a law that is absolutely necessary in the public interest, which is necessary for the protection of the travelling public and for the lives of the railway employees, and yet we can-

not get the Bill through on account of this quarrel between the power companies and other interests in the province of Ontario.
I am satisfied that if this amendment is carried it will not pass the Senate, because it has already been before the Senate; it was before the Senate this year, it was before the Senate last year, and the year before that. Perhaps the Senate would accept an amendment on the lines proposed by the hon. member for Shelburne and Queens. I would make the amendrnent a little shorter, hut it would have the same effect. The words that are not satisfactory to the municipality are these:
If any municipality complains to the Board that any company whether incorporated by special or other Act or authority of the Parliament of Canada is exercising its powers oppressively or in bad faith the Board may hear such complaint and if it sees fit supervise the exercise of such powers.
Some hon. members who have spoken, including, I think, the hon. member for Parkdale, have argued that the words "oppressively or in bad faith" mean practically nothing. I would suggest that subsection 5 be amended to read as follows:
(5) Any specific powers inconsistent with the provisions of this section and conferred on any company by any special or other Act or authority of the Parliament of Canada or of any province shall not ho affected by the provisions of this section; no such power shall be exercised except in accordance with terms of an order made by the Board after a hearing, at which hearing the municipality shall have the right to be heard: Provided always that whenever any company incorporated by special Act of the Parliament of Canada acquires the assets-

The amendment proposed by the minister deals with companies entering municipalities, and I am satisfied with the idea. But does it provide for the extension of the work of the company in a municipality in which it is now operating?

The minister evidently is willing to throw Toronto to the wolves. Provided this amendment that is moved by the hon. member for Parkdale does not apply to Toronto, he would be willing to accept it. As I understand this question, after listening to the debates in the Special Railway Committee, this company in 1902 got a charter from the Parliament of Canada. It was distinctly and well understood

that they had no right to distribute power in any city without the city's consent. There is absolutely no question albout that. Hansard shows it. Every member who spoke on the subject, and the minister in charge of the Bill, agreed that they were only getting the same power as other companies had been getting in the last year or two previous to that time. It was not understood that they had any special privileges other than the rights of transmission. If any municipality objected to their going through with their power line they could appeal to the Railway Commission, but there never was any intention on the part of Parliament or any one. else concerned that they should have the right to go into any municipality and distribute power at will. There was no thought at that time, nor is there now-and I doubt very much whether you could get a mover and seconder to-day in this Parliament, to a resolution for the purpose-to grant a perpetual franchise to a private corporation to go into any city in Canada and operate without the consent of that municipality. It seems preposterous, and undoubtedly it was not the .intention of Parliament at the time that they should have these powers. On the strength of the right which they had t.o develop power at Niagara Falls, transmit it to Toronto and other points, and sell it in Toronto to any one who had the franchise to distribute power, they contracted with the Toronto Light Company to furnish them power in Toronto at a certain price. The Toronto Electric Light Company had right to distribute power in the city for a limited number of years.
On the strength of the limited franchises of the Toronto Electric Light Company and the Toronto Street Railway Company, this company sold stocks and bonds, developed power and delivered it. They delivered it on the distinct understanding that they were selling it to two companies whose franchises would expire. They should therefore-I do not know whether they did or not-have put aside a sufficient amount out of their earnings to have redeemed the bonds at the termination of the franchises of the companies to which they were selling power. If they did not do that they should have done so. If they did not do that and the bondholders suffer any loss by the cancellation of this contract the shareholders who took dividends out of the company should pay them back into the company and that money should revert to the bondholders. The bondholders passed their money over in good faith with the know-

ledge that this company was selling power to the two Toronto companies each with a franchise which would terminate. There is no question in anybody's mind but that a wrong bas been done to the municipality. Every person is willing to right that wrong provided it does not hurt somebody else. We had eminent counsel here from all over the country talking on behalf of the bondholder. The bondholder, it was said, would lose if this amendment should carry. But there was not one of them who said what the bondholder would actually lose. When Mr. Beck was here in the interest of a million dollars worth of bonds, he made a very eloquent speech. When he started I asked him whom he represented and he said the bondholders. Vested interests: I have very little respect for them if they do not represent honest investment, and honest service to the community. I have no respect for the vested interest that is represented by the stock of this company. The interest that is represented by the bonds in the company should be protected by the stockholders. I think the bondholder could make the stockholder take out of his .pocket and return the dividends that he took out of that company knowing the franchise would expire.

I asked some of the gentlemen who appeared before the Committee for the prospectus on which they sold the bonds and my impression is they did not say they were selling bonds on the strength of the decision of the Privy Council. Is it not a fact that in
the offer made by Toronto to purchase the stock of the Toronto Electric Light Corn-pay "there was a clause that the electrical current in the future would not be supplied by the Toronto and Niagara Power Company but by the Hydro-Electric Company?

I would sit in the
gallery myself to hear this speech.

Well, I should hope the hon. member would sit in a different part from that to which my ideas are related just now. The question before the House and
the country is: How far is the Parliament of Canada going to stand for public (rights of all municipalities? Or is it going to stand for the vested interests which are behind these concerns? The hon. Minister of Public Works has made a strong appeal to the majesty of the law and to the respect which is owing to the Privy Council. I was in the service of the city of Toronto when part of this transaction occurred. The city gave to the Toronto Electric Light Company, which has an underground distribution, a contract to light their streets. That contract was for five years or under, and it gave the company the privilege for that period to put lighting poles on the streets. When the city could make other arrangements they terminated their contract with the company and ordered them to remove their poles. But [DOT] the company would not obey. So the city of Toronto proceeded through the courts until finally judgment was given in the Privy Council that the company were trespassers, as the hon. member for Kingston has explained. To an ordinary individual, such a judgment would be sufficient. Not so to this company. The Toronto Electric. Light Company immediately transferred their assets to the Toronto and Niagara Power Company-whose sensibilities so many of u:s are defending to-night-and then the Toronto and Niagara Power Company said: "Oh, well, we now own these poles; we have the right to plant them there, and there they will stay." For that reason, Mr. Chairman, I am going to support the amendment as moved by the hon. member for Parkdale. I am going to at least put myself upon the side of those who believe that in voting for

that amendment they are supporting the rights of the people. It is not the city of Toronto's battle; the battle affects every municipality in the Dominion of Canada from ocean to ocean. All along from the Niagara Power plant, we have the company's line passing through the city of St. Catherines, the city of Welland, the city of Hamilton, the town of Oakville, the town of Mimico and the city of Toronto -the whole line there already, and we have the possibilities of these competing distributing plants being extended not only in every municipality in Ontario, hut in every municipality in the whole Dominion. The vested interests may talk about the Hydro Electric in Ontario, but that undertaking was the outcome of the oppressive . measures of the Toronto and Niagara Power Company hitched up with the Toronto Electric Light Company, because they were in the position where they could supply or deny light and power to any firm they pleased; they could supply one factory with power, and the next factory in opposition to them would have to depend upon steam. real milk in the cocoanut, gentlemen. They expect to compel the city of Toronto to renew the franchise for the Toronto Street Railway. And the argument of the hon. Did the hon. gentleman understand me to say that I thought Parliament had any power to interfere with the contract between the Toronto and Niagara Power Company and the street railway or the Toronto Electric Light Company? because I want to tell him that I know
[Mr Sheard.]
too much about the constitution of this country to make such a statement. It is not true.

Mr. Chairman, I do not propose to detain the House at any great length at this hour. From the trend of the discussion one might gather the impression that the city of Toronto was the only municipality in the Dominion interested in this matter. But I can assure the House that I have no particular interest in the city of Toronto. However, I am interested generally in . the municipalities throughout the Dominion of Canada. The question at issue is that of dealing with the rights of these municipalities, the jurisdiction which they exercise over their streets, and the power of the Dominion of Canada to invade those rights. It seems to me that we should examine first the attitude of the Federal Government towards municipalities so far as transmission companies are concerned. That has been referred to several times to-night, but I ask the patience of the Committee while I refer to it again in order that we may see exactly what the stand of the Government has been on this question in the past.

There is no doubt that the legislation, from the earliest days down, admitted that the jurisdiction over the streets rested in some body other than the Dominion Government, whether the municipality, the province, or, as in the case of Ontario, the Hydro-Electric Commission. When that is conceded we must look at the attitude of the Dominion Government in its legislation dealing with this question. About the first clause of this kind we find is in an Act passed in 1899. I will read the clause:
When any company has power by any Act ot the Parliament of Canada to construct and maintain lines of telegraph or telephone or lines for the conveyance of light, heat, power or. electricity, such company may with the consent of the municipal council or other authority having jurisdiction over any highway, square or other public place, enter thereon for the purpose of exercising the said power, and as often as the company thinks proper may break up or open any highway, etc.
In that year they were required, whether they were corporations for the transmission of power or corporations for the sale and distribution of power in any municipality, to obtain the consent of the municipal council or other authority. That continued to be the law until 1903. The member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle) pointed out that the law at that time resolved itself into two branches, one governing the question of the transmission of power and the other governing the question of sale. The transmission of power was subject to the consent of the municipality, and if they refused, to the consent of the Board of Railway Commissioners. But when it came to the question of the sale of power, this Parliament was very jealous of the rights of municipalities and said that no company could go in unless they obtained the consent of the municipality by by-law, which is the most formal manner of obtaining that consent. That provision was subsequently re-enacted and continued down to 1917, when the Railway Act was revised. Now, the intention of Parliament is absolutely clear: That the rights of the municipalities are sacred and should not be encroached upon by any corporation without the consent of the municipality by by-law. In 1902 this company was incorporated. That an error was made is evident from the discussion which took place at that time. I quote from the remarks of Mr. Pringle:-
I understand that it means just what it expresses. All companies have to obtain the consent of a municipality before passing through it..
There is not the slightest thing in the discussion which took place on that occasion
to show that the intention of Parliament was to grant to this corporation any greater rights or any greater benefits than could be enjoyed by any other corporation in Canada. When they seek to establish that Parliament intended to give them greater rights I submit that the burden of proof is on them to show clearly that that was the intention of Parliament. So far as the legislation of this House was concerned, it remained practically in that position until 1917, when the Railway Act was revised by a special committee, passed by the House of Commons and sent to the Senate.
I take issue with the Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Carvell), who cast some ' reflection on the members of Parliament who saw fit to say that these rights should be restored to municipalities. I have the greatest respect for his honour, his integrity and his judgment; I believe that he is absolutely sincere when he says that these rights should not be interfered with. But I assure the hon. gentleman that while I have that high respect for him and that high estimate of him, I have just as great a respect for myself and just as high an estimate of myself and for my judgment and my action in voting in support of the amendment.
Hon. gentlemen talk about vested rights. Well, put it on the ground of vested rights, if you will, for the sake of -argument. We will eliminate. all question of dispute between the city of Toronto, the Toronto and Niagara Power Company and the HydroElectric. Under the Act the vested rights may be in the Toronto and Niagara Power Company, but the first vested rights in regard to the streets of these municipalities w-as either in the province or the -municipality, or, in Ontario, in the Hydro-Electric Commission. I ask the minister, does he stand here and say that it is dishonourable for Parliament to restore to municipalities rights which were deliberately taken from them without their knowledge, without their consent, without any consultation with them? When that Act was passed no doubt Parliament believed that they could exercise jurisdiction if any mistake was made. But I stand broadly on the principle that when the conflict comes between the eight million people in Canada and the Toronto and Niagara Power Company, if there must be sacrifice on the part of either, that sacrifice must he on the part of the corporation, not of the people who own and control the streets in the municipalities of this country.
But, Mr. Chairman, when we put it on that narrow ground of vested rights, I do not believe that we are placing it upon the



ground upon which it should be placed. When we talk of vested rights, about legislating away the rights this corporation got under the Act of 1902, we are overlooking the fundamental principle which should govern our action in this connection. It is not a matter of depriving a company of vested rights; it is not a matter of taking anything away from them. It is a matter of putting them in the class of public utilities in which all these transmission companies must come; and it is then for us to say whether as a Parliament we can exercise jurisdiction by controlling them. It is simply a question of control over a public utility corporation. Those people who argue that these contracts are very sacred must realize that during the last fifteen or twenty years one of the objects of Federal legislation has been to exercise control over public utilities and common carriers. Will any hon. gentlman in this Committee argue that because a railway company received a charter some years ago before any Railway Act was in force, we must not apply the Railway Act to that corporation? It is true that had the Act nbt been put in force the company might have had the privilege of charging double or treble the rates which are at present fixed by law. But we 'realized that these corporations, these utilities, are servants of the public, and notwithstanding any great concessions which they may have received in their original Act of incorporation they must be bound by the general laws of the country even though those laws may cut down the rates which they nnay charge for transportation, even though they may cut down the rates of a telephone company, or telegraph charges, which have already been cut down. We must realize that Parliament is supreme, and that when an injustice is being done to the public by these corporations in the legal exercise of their rights, Parliament must step in and the public must be protected. All we are asking in this case is simply that the Dominion Parliament shall exercise its proper functions, that it shall perform its duty to the public and step in so flar as this public utility is concerned, just as it proposes to step in under the other clauses of the Act. All we ask is that Parliament shall say to this company: "Notwithstanding you received your charter in 1902, you must be subject to the general laws of this country. We are going to control your rights to enter streets, but we are not going to take away your rights to sell and distribute power throughout the province of 
Ontario or the Dominion of Canada." Is there anything in this amendment which takes away from the company any specific rights which were granted to them under their charter? Is there even any suggestion of that in this amendment? Was there any suggestion of it in the Bill which was passed in 1917? I submit that the question to be answered by every man in this Committee, either on one alternative or the other, is, in the first place: Mus't the vested rights of the municipalities give way to the vested rights of private corporations which have been procured through error or misunderstanding? On the other alternative, you must ask yourself the question: Are we going to except one corporation in this country from control which can be justly exercised over it by Parliament? I think there is not a man in this House who asks himself that question honestly and conscientiously who can do otherwise than come to the conclusion that Parliament is supreme, and that this corporation must submit to the control of Parliament, no matter what the ultimate outcome nnay be, so long as the public interests are served.
The Minister of Public Works said what a bad lot of people we would be in this House if we passed this amendment, but on looking over the report of the special committee that was appointed in 1917 to consolidate and amend the Railway Act, I find that it was composed as follows: Messieurs Ames (Sir Herbert), Armstrong (Lambton), Bennett (Calgary), Blain, Car-veil, Cochrane, Cromwell, Donaldson, Graham, Green, Lapointe (Kamouraska), Lemieux, Macdonell, Meighen, Nesbitt, Oliver, Pugsley, Rainville, Sinclair and Turriff. Was that committee dishonourable? Did they do anything to damage the credit of the Dominion of Canada? Were they disloyal to the trust which was reposed in them by the people when they passed the amendment which was submitted to this House and later , went up to the Senate? Was the House of Commons in 1917, when it passed the section which we ask to have inserted in this Bill, dishonourable? I think that they could hold their heads as high, so far as business integrity and business morality is concerned, as this or any other Parliament in the history of Canada.
It is complained that we may have difficulty in getting this Bill through this session unless we very materially consent to the amendment of the Senate. But I submit this proposition: The House of Com-

mons is the elective body representing the people of the Dominion of Canada; the Senate is the body which has been appointed for life; and when it comes to a question of their judging on the morality of the House of Commons, I must say that I think the morality of the House of Commons will compare favourably with theirs. If legislation is being impeded in this conn try, it is not by the House of Commons, but by the autocratic body of the Senate which is not responsible to anybody and which looks better after the interests of private corporations than of the people whom we are elected to represent. I have very strong feelings upon this subject. Those men who passed that Act in 1917 had free and full discussion on it. They realized their duties and their obligations. Are we to pass judgment on them and say "You did something which was immoral so far as business obligations are concerned and you must accept the reprimand which has been delivered to you by the Senate of Canada"? So far as I am concerned I do not care to accept any reprimand which may have been handed by the Senate to the last Parliament. If we pass this amendment, I submit, it is the duty of the Senate to accept the Bill as we pass it, and if they do not accept it, then, I submit, it is the duty of the Government to bring down some restrictive legislation so that the will of the people cannot be thwarted by a body which is not responsible to the people.
'Mr. PARDEE:	I do not intend at this
late hour to go into the legal aspects of the case now before the Committee, as that has already been done very ably by several speakers who have preceded me. There is one thing I should like to say, however, and which I think this Committee ought to keep in mind all the time, and that is with respect to the argument that has been presented in favour of vested rights. We have heard it declaimed both in the Special Committee and in this House time and again that there were certain vested rights in regard to the bondholder. That may be very true; there are certain vested rights there. But I submit that although the bondholders may have vested rights, the first and only thing that we, as representatives of the people, ought to consider are the vested rights of the people. There has been much sympathy expressed for the bondholder. He has been held up time and again as having put his money into this venture, and now, forsooth, because certain things may hap-198i
pen in a legislative way, he may not get back his money. As far as the hondholder is concerned, he has a right to be looked after by this Committee and by this House, if he has not' already looked after himself, but the peculiar circumstances of this case must all be taken into consideration.
We have here four companies, all mixed up. They are under different names and under different heads, but, nevertheless, these four companies are under one control. There is not one of them that is not subservient to one set of men. True it is, the Toronto and Niagara Power Company were pioneers, but from what I gathered in the Committee and here, that pioneer work amounted to this:	The Toronto and Niagara Power Company issued Jl,500,000 worth of bonds, and $700,000 worth of stock, and there they stopped; that was the end of it, so far as the issuing of stock and bonds under that charter was concerned. These men left this House knowing and being absolutely satisfied in their own minds that they were coming under the Railway Act and had no greater rights than that Act gave them. Under these circumstances, what happened? They went on and sold $1,500,000 bonds, and issued $700,000 worth of stock. Some one then, looking over the Act, lawyer-like, I will admit, said there is a flaw; here is a chance where we may go on and carry out our undertaking; that undertaking may be carried out irrespective of the clauses of the Railway Act and consequently irrespective of the rights of the municipalities. The case was taken to the lower court and decided in favour of the company, then to the Court of Appeal who upset the judgment of the lower court. They took it to the Privy Council and again the judgment of the lower court was upheld. The Privy Council held that the company had the right to go on and across the streets of the municipalities. It appears to me to be a most significant thing that during the course of the various states of litigation that took place in the lower court, in the Court of Appeal and in the Privy Council, bonds were sold.

I do not purpose to speak at any great length on this matter because I think it is unnecessary, but I think if would be well if we got before us clearly what it is that the hon. member for Park-dale asks us to vote upon. It seems to me to be a very simple matter, and I really do not see why it should call for so much argument. The proposition of the hon. member for Parkdale is this:	Are you going to put all the electric power companies of Canada under one class of legislation, or are you going to leave one to run at large?

That is the proposition clearly and concisely put. In the interests of the municipalities and of the people of the country, what ever may have been the rights given in 1902 to the Toronto and Niagara Power Company the time has come when there should be one class of legislation governing all companies of this kind. Section 374 provides for electric companies in this country to have through transmission lines for power and transmission. In the case of refusal by the municipality to allow transmission through the municipality, there is provision for application to the Railway Board, and in the case of distribution they must apply to the municipality, and if the municipality refuses, the matter there ends. That is the legislation which it is proposed to apply to all companies at present in existence. It has been suggested by my hon. friend from Vancouver, that there may be other companies in the same line as the Toronto and Niagara Power Company. What I most strongly urge is this:
If there are any such-which I do not believe, because this matter has been under discussion by Parliament for practically three years and it has received a great deal of newspaper notoriety-and if there are any others, we would have heard of them. But assuming that there are, is that not all the more reason for making this legislation apply to every company in this country and not allowing these companies (at large to exercise their rights when and wherever they may desire as against the rights of the municipalities? It is suggested that this is not the proper place to deal with this matter but .somebody should take it upon himself to apply to Parliament to ask to have the Toronto and Niagara Power Company's charter amended at some other time and on some other occasion. In view of the fact that the Toronto and Niagara Power Company took their charter with, what every member of this House admits, the full knowledge and belief that the Railway Act of that day applied to the charter, we are doing them no harm now, they having been allowed to run free for a few years, and having got rights that they never expected, by putting them under the same legislation as every other power company in this country.
It is suggested by the Minister of Railways (Mr. Reid) that the province of Ontario has passed improper legislation in that regard because it does not allow municipalities to pass bylaws without the consent of the Lieutenant Governor in Council.
It does not seen to me it is the duty of this House to sit in review on the legislation of the province of Ontario. That is a matter for the people of Ontario to deal with just as it is a matter for the people of Quebec or for any of the other provinces to deal with matters that come within their jurisdiction. We are not here as a court of review to sit in judgment upon the province of Ontario or any other province but we are here to pass legislation in the interest of the people of Canada and we should leave them to fight out their own provincial rights in their own provinces.
The only other matter that has been raised for our consideration is the question of the rights of bondholders. I fancy that the picture of two of our ministers weeping over the rights of these bondholders will go down in history because I do not believe that the rights of the bondholders will be affected very much. The suggestion made by Mr. Beck was that in so far as he knew no bondholder would be affected. I do not believe there is one particle of doubt that these bonds are all amply secured. We are told that this company has a 250,000 horse-power development at Niagara Falls. We are told	that they were
the pioneers in electrical development and we are asked to sympathize with their pioneer efforts. The pioneers in the development of electrical power, and the people who spent large sums of money, were the Niagara Falls Po.weT Company. They were at it for ten years on the American side iand they spent millions in perfecting the machinery which enabled Niagara's power to be chained up. The next power company was the Ontario Power Company, an American concern. The Toronto Niagara Power Company were the third set of people to go into that line of business and when they began the development of electrical power it was fairly well known and understood. But there was something that was not known in 1902 and that was the extent to which electricity was going to he developed and the vital importance that it was going to be to the people. We had very scant knowledge as to the protection that should be given to the people in connection with a matter of that kind. Every effort was made at that time that reasonably could be made, both by the late Mr. Clarke and Mr. (now Sir Edmund) Osier, to see that proper protection was given to the municipalities. As my hon. friends who support the amendment have said, it is perfectly and obviously clear that the gentlemen who got this

charter, and who are here to-night, knew perfectly well that they received that charter subject to the rights of municipalities in connection with their own interests.
Is Parliament supreme in matters of this kind? What are the rights of franchise holders as compared with the rights of the people? A franchise is merely a part of a public right given by Parliament to certain people to administer. It may be changed and altered. It is not a vested right; it is simply a permission to certain people to exercise definite public powers that belong to Parliament and to that extent these powers must be absolutely subject to the legislative control of Parliament. I am satisfied that hon. members will find that when they go back home to their constituents in the different municipalities, towns and cities, they will find it hard to explain why they voted for alleged vested rights and financial interests as against the rights and interests of the municipalities of their own constituents.

Mr. Chairman, this question has been so fully, ably and comprehensively dealt with from the legal standpoint by the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Mowat) and others that I do not feel called upon to say very much. I have not very much sympathy with the bondholders. They are a class of people who, as was said by the hon. member for Lamb-ton (Mr. Pardee) are well able to take care of themselves, and in this case they evidently did. What has impressed me is that there is not a man here to-night who will say that the legislation which gave this company the powers it enjoys is legislation that would he adopted at the present time. This House made a very serious mistake in 1902 and the effect of that mistake is to deprive the city of Toronto, and all the municipalities concerned, of the control of their streets. That was recognized at the time this legislation was before the House.
I remember very distinctly that the Canadian union of municipalities, representing every municipality from the Atlantic to the Pacific, sent their representatives down here to voice their opposition to the measure. They did everything in their power at that time to resist the attempt of this company to get the rights which they sought. In addition to all that has been quoted as to the understanding of Parliament in regard to the application of the general Railway Act to this company, I am informed that the chairman of the Railway Committee of that day, Mr. Mahlon

Cowan, wrote a letter to one of the mayors of a western town declaring that the company that was being chartered would come under the general Act. That being the case and the first offence being to deprive the municipalities of their vested rights, that initial fault ought to be corrected by this Bouse to-night. The amendment proposed by my hon. friend from Parkdale makes that correction and I submit that this Committee ought to adopt that amendment and put all the electrical companies in the same position in regard to the Act.
