For my part, I cannot bring myself to think that it is proper, notwithstanding all that has been said, that when this charter has heen granted and when over $30,000,000 have been spent in the undertaking-the statement has never been challenged, it was made over and over again in the select committee and nobody challenged it, and I think we may fairly say that it is certain

there is in this undertaking over $30,000,000 -that we should jeopardize, or, as has been suggested by the editor of Saturday Nigin,, confiscate that property. I cannot bring myself to do that; at all events noi if there is any reasonable way of protecting the municipality and at the same time the company.
Reference has been made to bondholders, and to the million and a half dollars' worth of bonds. It would seem to me that it was hardly necessary to argue that proposition. It is said that this particular company issued bonds to the extent of only $1,500,000. But surely when we understand that it forms an important part of three distinct systems, namely, the generating plant at the Falls, the transmission plant, and the distribution plant, we must realize that to take any one of those away would render the balance worthless. If you say to this company or to any other company, "You cannot enter any municipality without consent, which consent may be withheld without any reason whatever," you surely make useless the whole undertaking. And that is what we are asked to do.
If I was now being called upon to cast a vote as to whether or not I would support a charter such as was granted in 1902, it goes without saying that.I would not think of doing so. But the position to-day is very different from the position then. It was only in 1899 that the idea of obtaining consent of the municipalities was first determined upon by Parliament, and the very idea of obtaining consent was fresh in the minds of the members of Parliament in 1902. Therefore if it was thought proper to make this company get the consent of every municipality before proceeding with its undertaking, surely Parliament would have said so in plain English. It seems to me we are casting a serious reflection upon the members of Parliament of 1902 when we quietly sit down to amend their work, because from a word or two that was dropped from three of four members we suggest the other members did not know what they were doing. In 1899 that policy of consent was adopted, it was everybody's mind, and there was no suoh provision put in the Special Act. In 1903 in the consolidation it was again inserted, but there, was no saving clause put in the legislation then, and in the year after this charter went through, and they knew of that mistake, why do we not find in the consolidation some saving clause indicating that so far as this company was concerned the rights obtained by this charter-which

I admit is an omnibus, wide open, perpetual charter-were granted under misapprehension? Why did we not on the first opportunity the year after take occasion to correct the mistake made? It was not done, it was not dealt with in any subsequent consolidations and amendments. It is said that as a matter of fact this was raised as far back as 1912, and that because of the war and of the fact that the Railway Bill did not go through in 1917, the matter has been dragging along ever since. But there is no doubt that this very charter was used in the floatation of some $9,000,000 worth ol bonds-at all events, that is the uncontradicted evidence before the Committee- after the decision of the Privy Council, and how any one can argue or suggest that a bondholder would then be purchasing bonds with any doubt as to the position of the company is beyond my comprehension. We had the court of last resort outlining the powers of that company, and there was no chance of varying those powers unless Parliament itself was to abrogate what it did in 1902. Consequently on the strength of that charter $9,000,000 worth further bonds were sold. Are we to abrogate those rights entirely? Surely not.
The suggestion I have to make later, if this amendment is defeated, it seems to me would protect the company and the municipalities; and I do not think that any municipalities outside, we will say, two or three hundred miles of the Niagara plant need have any fear of invasion by this company so far as their streets are concerned. Without a shadow of doubt the company was originally incorporated for the purpose of generating and transmitting electricity from Niagara to Toronto. I have not much doubt that it was formed for the purpose of supplying current to the street railway and the electric light company, which was a convenient way of disposing of the current, much more so than setting up their own poles.
If the company wanted to go along a street where there were already telephone poles, street railway poles, and hydro poles, the board could say to them, " No, if you wish to tan the locality that is reached by this street you must go up to a further cross street where there are no poles and find a way there." In that way' I think we would do away with the greatest evil, the placing along the street of endless poles.

The hon. member for Parkdale has brought in a resolution by way of amendment that would, to my mind, as has been stated by others, amount to confiscation of practically fifty per cent at least of the value of this company's assets.
The bonds to that extent would suffer. When we are settling the rights and powers and privileges of this company, I cannot, as a member of this House, having regard to the judgment of the Chancellor of Ontario and of the Privy Council of England, lightly ignore a -position of that kind and vote for the confiscation of the money of any body, whether he lives in Canada, England, United States, or France. I am not sure that this House has been serious enough in viewing this question, I might quote in addition to what the member for South Simcoe (Mr. Boys) quoted, from an article published in Toronto quoting the London Saturday Review:
The recent attempt to have the Railway Act so amended that it would, in effect, have made the charter of the Toronto and Niagara Power Company valueless, and would, at the same time, have betrayed the investors who, in good faith, placed their money in this undertaking, met with its just deserts at the hands of a Committee of the House of Commons. Such attempts at confiscatory legislation are not being overlooked in England, whose moneyed men furnished so much of the capital which went to build up just such enterprises in Canada. For1 instance, a recent issue of the London Saturday Review had this to say:
"Canadian and Australian Governments have taken to an ugly and dishonest trick of recent years, which, unless abandoned, will effectually cut off the inflow of British capital. It is this. A syndicate or company of shareholders, as a rule British, are given powers by the local legislature to build and equip some great .undertaking, such as a railway, or an electrical power plant. When it has been completed and found to be running at a profit, the Colonial Legislature arms the State with powers to run a rival undertaking, which, owing to Government patronage ruins the private concern. This is practically what the Government of Western ^Australia has done to the Midland Railway. This is apparently what the Government of Ontario is trying to do to the Electric Development Company of Ontario, which hqs brought an action against the Attorney-General and the Hydro-Electric Power Commission of Ontario. The Lieutenant-Governor of Ontario has done his best to defeat the Development Company by a legal technicality, which the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council has very properly disallowed."
Let me ask, is there any truth in what the Privy Council said? Was this Toronto and Niagara Power Company a pioneer? The member for South Toronto (Mr. Sheard) says they were not. In return, I assert that no company established on the United States side of the Niagara Fails had trans-

mitted electricity any distance beyond the city of Buffalo-a matter of far less than half a hundred miles. At that time the electrical experts of the world were in doubt as to the possibility of the commercial transport of electricity at a profit. Nikola Tesla said one thing and Edison said another. This company had the courage and the nerve which made the Privy Council say it was a pioneer; therefore, it got wide powers. I freely concur in what has been stated here, that on the floor of this House there wias a discussion as to whether or not the powers were so wide. But the company interpreted its own statute; the company's solicitors undertook at a certain stage to say what those powers were. Having taken, the Act and studied it and found out what their powers were, they, as they had the right to do, went on and issued $9,000,000 worth more bonds. Why, it is said that when this company first got into Toronto, the city was ablaze with glory and joy because a real, splendid new enterprise had been, brought to their door and they were going to be flooded with electric light. They were pleased with it and they continued to be pleased with it for many years. Not until the HydroElectric, a provincial utility, came into the field, was any objection raised or antipathy shown to this particular company. Now, I am rather inclined to view the HydroElectric Commission as one of the greatest public utilities that Ontario has. Bo much do I think of it that I am inclined to belittle the arguments of hon. gentlemen who fear the competition of this company against the Hydro Electric, which has the public purse, the public pulse and the public generally behind it; which is carrying on business in Ontario not for profit, but for the benefit of the people. When men speak of this small company fighting its way on its own money-borrowed, it is true,-most of it-against one of the greatest provinces in this Dominion, with its purse outpouring to the splendid Hydro Electric utility, I say it is rather stretching an argument to assert that the public right is being interfered with. I do not believe that any public right is going to be hurt by this cbmpany. The Hydro Electric is in nearly every part of western Ontario to-day; there is no need of another company coming in. In the course of time, when the Hydro Electric is fully developed, it can take up a further field in eastern Ontario. I do not see why they cannot compete with an overflowing purse behind them.

Let it be remembered just here that the Hydro, in spite of all its good and of all its usefulness to the public, has never yet developed a single horsepower; it has bought its power from companies like this, and others. It is not a pioneer, and I decline to accept the argument that to support the law as found by the Chancellor of Ontario and the Privy Council in England is plain treason to the Hydro Electric Commission and to the people of Ontario.
I do not believe that the people of Ontario will accept such an argument. They are as fair and as broad-spirited and as equitable and as manly as any people in the Dominion. I do not think that their view is so narrow and restricted as the view represented by some arguments that have been offered here to-day. The Hydro has a splendid body of engineers to regulate it, and they are taking up large developments. It cost $15,000,000 to develop Chippewa creek, I hear a whisper, "$30,000,000"; be careful that it is not $50,000,000. In any case, they are prepared to go into the field, and that any Act of this Parliament should be passed that would operate as confiscation is to say the least, unreasonable. No	sensible man can deny that
there would be a loss. In two years the Toronto Electric Railway Company goes over to the city of Toronto, and they will use Hydro-Electric, provincial power. There is 40,000 horse-power gone at one swoop. It may be that there are worse things in the world than a little competition, even for a publicly-owned utility. Every one in the country is not buoyed up with the assurance of the final and ultimate success of our National railways under federal ownership, or of Hydro-Electric under provincial ownership. We all hope they will succeed, for the interest and the benefit of the people, but no man knows. Consequently, to put our eggs all in one basket might be the worst thing that ever happened.
Let me point out one thing to the committee. This Toronto and Niagara Power Company has 27,000 customers in Toronto, notwithstanding the fact that it charges more for its service than the Hydro-Electric charges. Their argument is that the people pay more because their system is better and more efficient, and the service consequently better. Charging more against a big corporation like the Hydro, yet holding 27,000 subscribers-that is not competition in the ordinary sense. That is not bidding down to. make Hydro go lower. Only last week the Hydro knocked 20 per cent off all municipal charges in the province of Ontario,
and they can easily do it. I cannot support the amendment of the hon. member for Parkdale. I believe it would be confiscation. I feel that the temper of the House compels me to support the amendment proposed by the minister, because he has left some remnant of this company intact, as I understand it. If I am wrong, it may be said hereafter that that was the understanding I had. I do not know that it is wise fior us to accept what was said in debate in preference to the deliberate judgment of the highest court in the realm. The Act is the thing. It stands there to be scrutinized, and I think we should hesitate before creating a precedent here to-day upon data that is not quite sufficient to warrant the precedent being established. Mention has been made of the hon. Mr. Beck of New York. Hon. gentlemen may not remember everything he said, but one thing that impressed itself very strongly upon me was this sentence: "Canada must be a borrowing public. The United States is a lending public." England may not be a lending public for many years to come, and we may in the future require to raise money on the public credit. To raise money, the public credit must stand high, and the public credit springs from the fount of Parliament here. If this Parliament enacts legislation that goes to foreign lands with the hall mark of shame upon it, so that the credit of Canada is impaired, then if the amendment of the hon. member for Parkdale carries we may regret for many years to come that Parliament took that stand, probably without mature consideration and in the heat of a summer evening.

As a member of the
Special Committee on this Bill I wish to say a few words. I have listened to all the arguments on this question pro and con of the most capable lawyers probably in this country for four times, 'and they have all amounted to practically the same thing each time. Going back to the granting of the franchise to this company in 1902, we were told this afternoon, and have been told time and again before, that the Railway Committee of that day did not know what they were doing. I do not think we have any right to assume that any more than we have a right to_ assume that the Railway Committee of this day does not know what it is doing. As a matter of fact, a good deal of reference has been made to some of the objections raised by Mr. Osier and Mr. Clarke at that time, and yet the

Committee passed the Bill in spite of these gentlemen's objections. That looks to me as if the Railway Committee of that day knew exactly what they were doing. I can construe it in no other way. The objections were m/ade, and still the Railway Committee of that day passed the Bill. Furthermore, the mayor of Toronto at that time, Mr. Urquhart, wrote a letter to the Toronto'-City Council and the Controllers pointing out that the Mackenzie and Mann people had been given exactly the powers which the Privy Council decided had been given to them. There was no objection from the Toronto City Council that we ever heard of in the Railway Committee.
As far as the bonds are concerned, it has been said that $1,500,000 of bonds were issued by the transmission company, which was the first company formed, I understand. These were never sold, but were taken up by the development company. Afterwards, the development company built the transmission line to Toronto. The Committee never heard of any objection to that from any of the municipalities. The lines were built without any trouble until they invaded North Toronto. In the meantime the development company had sold some $7,000,000 of bonds. There was a question before the special committee as to whether value was received for the bonds, but there was no objection made before the special committee by the solicitors for the city of Toronto that the money was not properly expended. Some $34,000,000 or $35,000,000 was expended and $27,000,000 of bonds . were issued altogether, I understand. When the trouble did arise there was an appeal to Chancellor Boyd, who was one of the most capable judges in the province of Ontario. He gave a decision in favour of the company. The first bonds had been sold previous to that decision. After that decision more bonds were issued, but they were held over until the appeal had been heard by the Privy Council, and when the Privy Council, the court, of last resort in the Empire, gave their decision these bonds that had been issued, $9,000,000 worth, were sold. Nobody can tell me that the solicitors who were engaged to investigate the title that was to be the security for these bonds did not take the franchise as the main security, because anybody who has ever tried to sell public utility bonds know that you cannot sell them unless you have a proper franchise. The two franchises that hon. gentlemen say were the security for these bonds were both limited franchises, and I do not believe that the
fMr. Nesbitt. 1
purchasers of the bonds would have bought them except for the fact that the franchise was behind the bonds. That may be disputed, but I have listened to all the arguments four times now, and I have never heard any reason given to change my mind that that was the main source of credit for the sale of these bonds.
The hon. member for Parkdale this afternoon made an argument I have never heard before on this question. He said that it was a mistake of the law clerk that was responsible for the franchise being granted. I have sat on the Railway Committee since I have been a member of Parliament, and ,1 know that the Committee always look carefully over the Bill to see that the law clerk has drawn it properly before they vote on it.
That has been my experience in any Railway Committee on which I have sat, and I believe that the Railway Committee of that day knew what they were doing just as much as the Railway Committee of this day does. It is said, quite truly, that we would not grant a franchise of that kind today, but you must not think of it for to-day. You must go back seventeen years ago when the distribution or the transmission of power was in its infancy. A power company had been, established at Niagara Falls before that time, but as my hon. friend from North Perth said, the furthest transmission that had taken place up to \that time was to Buffalo, by the International Power Company, which I believe has since changed its name. There is no doubt that, whatever faults there might have been in the franchise at that time, tfhe city council wer5 then glad to get this company to transmit power to Toronto. It has been said that these people have got their poles on the streets of Toronto contrary to the order of the Privy Cbuncil that they should be removed. These poles were ordered to be removed, and why has the city of Toronto not enforced that order of the Privy Council? Because, as the member for North Perth says, there are 27,000 people using this power in the city of Toronto, and I do not think they would be in favour of having these poles removed. That must be the reason why the city has not ordered their removal before now. They have stopped this company from lighting the streets of Toronto, but private people of Toronto still patronize the company. I shall not dwell on this phase of the subject further, but what strikes me forcibly is this:	These
people got the franchise and proceeded to sell bonds, and my experience has been that

if a private individual breaks a contract- at least if any man breaks a contract with me-he is not trusted any more by me. A man may break a contract with me once, but never a second time, because I will not trust him, and I believe that that is the case with businessmen throughout the length and breadth of tlhis land. What has built up the trade of the British Empire more than the fact that the people with whom she traded could depend on the goods which they received being according to representation? If a man lies to me about any particular thing, he may deceive me once, but it is my fault if he deceives me twice. Some one, I think the hon. member for Park-dale, talked this afternoon about our being honest, and I could not help thinking when I heard him whether it was the intention that this Parliament of Canada, the representatives of the people of this country, should be asked ito break a solemn contract and discredit us in the eyes ol the financial world. There can be no other interpretation than that, no matter how you may camouflage the legal aspect of the case. We have had a considerable lot of legal talk and for four years I have listened to it. But so far as I am personally concerned I look at the matter from one standpoint. If we pass the amendment as moved by the hon. member for Parkdale we practically confiscate these people's interests. There is no question about that. The bonds may or may not be good, but we have no right to confiscate any proper interests that have been built up with the legal endorsation of the Parliament of this country. And if all the lawyers in the United States and Canada were to talk to me about the legal aspects of the question, I could not consider it from any other standpoint than that we have no right to break a contract once it is made, and that we should stand by it even though it costa us something. I am as perfectly willing as any man to protect the municipalities, and I think the amendment suggested by the Minister of Railways fully protects the municipalities where these people have not entered into business; and it fully protects the municipality of Toronto as regards the future. It has been said that this company has Dominion-wide power and that from Halifax to Vancouver they can go into any municipality and occupy the streets. But after all we must give credit to the company for having some common sense. There would be no object in going into any muni-cioality unless the proposition would pay. If the city could not get power for less than
they were being supplied by the existing corporation, there is no fear, ,n my judgment, of this or any other company going into any municipality. I do not know of any municipality that would not welcome any corporation that could sell them power cheaper than they are getting at the present day. That is true of any municipality as it is in the case of individuals. The fact is, no matter with what legal phraseology it is surrounded: There people were granted the franchise and sold bonds. Some one said this afternoon that there was no proof that any of the bonds were sold out of Canada. But suppose that to be the case, is that any reason why we should confiscate the interests of the people of Canada? As a matter of fact, it was stated before the special committee time and again that these bonds were sold in England, France and the United States. The great majority of them were sold there, but even if they were not, is there any justification in our confiscating their value? By all means no. If they were sold in Canada, that is all the more reason why we should protect the interests of the people who held them. I am perfectly willing to see either the minister's clause inserted to protect the municipalities where these people are not now operating, or to accept the proposed amendment of my hon. friend from South Simcoe. But let us not confiscate the rights of any one and have the people of the world say that they cannot invest money in this country without running the risk of con-fiiscation.
The Committee divided on the amendment of Mr. Mowat.
Amendment agreed to, yeas 56, nays 52.

I was paired with the leader of the Opposition (Mr. McKenzie), otherwise I would have voted for the amendment.
Mr. MoMASTER: I should not have voted, Mr. Chairman; I was paired.

I did not want to make two mouthfulls of this but the next amendment is to the latter part of subclause 5. The Senate understood that this company was to buy out the Toronto Electric Eight Company. Now it seems to me that that is not so. I propose to move an amendment to change the latter part of the subclause and this will be subclause 6: I therefore beg to move:
That subsection 5 of section 374 be amended
by striking out all the words in the last eleven
lines from, and inclusive of, the word "pro-

vided" to the end of the section and substituting the following as a new subsection 6:
(6) If any company heretofore incorporated by Special Act or other authority of the Parliament of Canada has acquired, or shall acquire assets or any part thereof, or the right to the possession or use of the assets or any part thereof, of any company or person operating a 'system for the distribution of light, heat, power or electricity, in any town, city, village or township, then in every such case the company so acquiring such assets shall carry out with the municipality all the obligations, in respect to the said assets whether arising under contract or in any other manner, of the company from which the said assets have been or shall be acquired.
Section as amended, agreed to.

I think that completes all the clauses of the Bill. However, I would like to ask the committee to take up clauses 25 and 27 and make the changes in them that I shall propose. These are two clauses in reference to the employees of the Board of Railway Commissioners who are not now under the Civil Service Act. This will bring them under the Act. I therefore beg to move the reconsideration of section 25.
Motion agreed to.

I beg to move:
That section 25 be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
Such other officers, clerks, and employees as are necessary for the proper conduct of the business of the Board may be appointed in accordance with the provisions of the Civil Service Act 1918, and of any Acte in amendment thereof.

Amendment agreed to.
Mr. J. D. REID moved the reconsideration of section 27.
Motion agreed to.

I beg to move that section 27 be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
27. The officers, clerks and employees attached to the Board may be paid out of such money as may be appropriated by Parliament for the purpose.
The minister says "such other officers." That evidently excepts some. Who are those that are excepted ?
Section 25 excepted all officers employed by the Board of Railway Commissioners.

The amendment says "such other officers," meaning that there are some who will be appointed by the Civil Service Commission and others who will not be?
[Mr. Mowat.J
There are some officers such as Mr. Spencer. He is a special officer or inspector. They must all come under the Civil Service Commission, the same as the special officers in any other department.
Amendment agreed to.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall I report the Bill ?
Before you leave the Chair, Mr. Chairman, I would like to refer again to section 325.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Before referring to section 325 it will be necessary for the hon. gentleman to have the unanimous consent of the Committee. Is it the unanimous will of the Committee that the hon. member he allowed to revert to section 325 of the Bill?

I can go on with it now or wait until the third reading. It will take me a few minutes to explain it, but if the Committee do not wish me to go on to-night I shall defer what I have to say until the third reading. The amendment to section 325 has the effect of practically wiping out all agreements made between municipalities and the railway companies fixing rates in those municipalities. It also has the effect of wiping out an appeal which is now pending to the Supreme Court. 1 want to explain these things to the Committee, but if you would prefer me to do it on the third reading I should be glad to postpone what I have to say. It is so late now that I do not like to keep the Committee, but if you wish me to go ahead I am prepared to do so.
I have no objection, but I do not like to ask the Committee to remain.
That is the way I feel, too.
Does the hon. member wish to have the clause opened up again?
Yes.
I would not like to have the clause opened up again. Rather than have the clause opened I would prefer that you bring it up on the third reading.

I will take it up on the third reading, then.
Bill reported.
